#6810. Plestia Alaqad Sees the World

The photojournalist talks about the making of her latest book, The Eyes of Gaza

“The hardest part was having something as intimate and personal as a diary become public,” says Plestia Alaqad of her decision to publish her diary-memoir, The Eyes of Gaza. The book details the harrowing first weeks after October 7 in Gaza as a young Palestinian journalist. Alaqad studied new media and journalism at Eastern Mediterranean University in Cyprus before returning to her home in 2022. Intending to educate the world about her city, she did not know she would end up reporting the first stages of the genocide.

Alaqad’s reporting situated herself as a voice for the ordinary. In the first few days, she spoke to her neighbors and local children. Her reporting appeared mostly on her Instagram account, which grew to a little over 2 million followers, with many of her images republished by the BBC, The New York Times, PBS NewsHour, and The Washington Post. Even through the chaos and the expulsion of over 100,000 Gazans in the first few days, according to UNHCR, which Alaqad also recounts in her memoir, there are moments of tenderness caught by her and everyday Gazans she would meet and talk to. Her style of reporting is grounded in a sense of familiarity, narrating the everyday in extraordinary circumstances. She made connections with people in a way that makes you feel like you were alongside her, drinking tea with the local tetas and jiddos, watching the violence and the world collapse around you.

Alaqad left Gaza for Lebanon, where she is completing her master’s degree. During the course of our interview, she spoke openly with me about the loneliness of the isolation of being a witness, forever changed by the devastation.

One of my favorite things about Gaza is the people and the sense of community. For example, the relationship between my neighbors and I. I’ve been living in the Al -Waleed Building since I was almost four years old, and I know all my neighbors. Like Dana, who lived next door next to me—it was like having a sister and best friend nearby at all times. Whenever I needed anything, I just knocked at Dana’s door. If I needed help picking out an outfit, if I needed help replying to messages, even if I was just bored and I wanted someone to hang out with, it was always Dana who I turned to. There’s something about Gaza that just is home to me. There is simplicity and a love for life in Gaza that I haven’t seen elsewhere in the world. So being born and raised there always meant having loving and supportive people around me.

There’s more to us than being occupied. We’re full of talent and art we never got the time to make, because we’re too busy worrying if the people we love will still be alive tomorrow. That’s what pushes me to keep writing.

I’m interested in writing and telling stories of people. I recently interviewed Renad Atallah and wrote a piece about her for The New Arab. Also, one of my favorite pieces I wrote was an interview with Alaa Abu Diab, a one-of-a-kind comedian, for The National.

As of recently, I started my newsletter on Substack, where I share a personal essay every week on Gaza, girlhood, friendship, and everything in between. My ultimate hope would be to tell stories about a free Palestine one day. And as a journalist, I’ll always see my work as incomplete without going back to Gaza and continuing to tell Palestinian stories from the ground. And hopefully work on an international level and tell stories of people who suffered because of war and conflicts in other countries.

I enjoy reading nonfiction books and memoirs because I love learning about people and their experiences. I remember reading Anne Frank’s diary in middle school.… I remember how it made me feel and the impact it had on me.

I have also always been drawn to personal writings, like Franz Kafka’s letters and the letters between Ghassan Kanafani and Ghada al-Samman. I think I’m a very curious person by nature, and I’m interested in understanding what is happening in people’s minds, and if I get the chance to read strangers’ diaries, I wouldn't say no. That curiosity is something that inspired me.

Growing up, I always had a diary. It was me and my purple diary against the world.… For me, journaling has always been my safe space in the world. It’s the one place where I can write whatever I want without feeling judged. That’s honestly why I wanted to create Neya [Alaqad’s creative brand], which is an Arabic word that means intention. The first product will be a journal, of course, and it will come in four different colors. Each journal has a small, kind reminder on the hardcover and little sweet quotes throughout the pages because I wanted to create something that is personal and safe, something you would want to come back to and share your thoughts in. For me, journaling has always been where I can reconnect with myself. I hope Neya can become that for other people too: a small space where they can pause, reflect, and reconnect with themselves.

The hardest part was having something as intimate and personal as a diary become public. Something that was once only mine suddenly was in the hands of people from all around the world. I always try to think about the impact it could have on others, and I’m grateful that this time we get to tell our own stories rather than having our stories told on our behalf. I’m also grateful for the readers around the world who have read The Eyes of Gaza and are making the effort to educate themselves about Palestine.

I often feel like I am living in two worlds. On one hand, I have the opportunity to do things that many people back home cannot access freely, such as pursuing my education and continuing my master’s degree. On the other hand, I carry the weight of knowing what is happening to my people and my land, without having any superpower to stop it.

I always try to stay honest and true to myself, and I try to take people through this journey with me online. I share the contradictions, the pain, and the moments of hope. What it’s like trying to process the experience of having your homeland bombed, your city erased, and your people murdered, while also surviving and trying to make sense of the world outside. It is something that is difficult to put into words.

It feels like time has frozen in Gaza, while the rest of the world continues moving forward. And for those of us away from home, we are constantly trying to live between these two realities.

Gaza is a place where contradictions exist side by side. You see unimaginable grief, but you also see people trying to find meaning and strength in the middle of that suffering.

The Eyes of Gaza captures these contradictions. On one page, sadness may take over, while on another, hope emerges. Ultimately, I believe that when people experience powerful emotions, they are often moved to take action.

#6809. Study: Sign-In Problems Are Primary Drivers of Help Desk Tickets

Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network issues can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a new study from ControlUp.

Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations company identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) issues as major drivers of support demand.

At one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems. Meanwhile, 87% of network and phone tickets were reassigned between teams, compared with 20% of account tickets.

MFA enrollment and re-enrollment problems appeared at 40% of organizations, with one in five linking these issues to employees replacing or upgrading their phones. Virtual desktop problems appeared at 55% of organizations analyzed.

Traditional phone support remained a major channel for IT assistance.

Among organizations that recorded how support requests were submitted, 57% reported that phone calls accounted for approximately two-thirds or more of contacts. At one organization, that figure reached 99%.

Machine-generated tickets from monitoring, security, backup, and patching systems appeared at half of the organizations studied. At 15%, automated tickets represented between 25% and 50% of all requests.

The research covered enterprises across retail, healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, construction, energy, and IT services.

ControlUp said the findings highlight the need to evaluate recurring problems and their operational impact rather than relying solely on ticket volume and resolution speed.

"IT organizations have traditionally measured support performance by how quickly they close tickets, but that doesn't tell the whole story," said Simon Townsend, senior vice president of marketing and office of the CTO at ControlUp.

"A password reset that takes a few minutes and an infrastructure failure that disrupts an entire location shouldn't carry the same operational weight."

For more information, go to the ControlUp site.

#6806. The Beyond Devastating ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Ending, Explained

Crying too hard at the end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to fully grasp those final scenes? It can happen to the best of us. Let’s break down the ending of Sunrise on the Reaping to make sure you didn’t miss anything, including some of the things that Suzanne Collins’ book explains in a tiiiiiny bit more detail.

It should come as no surprise that Haymitch wins the Hunger Games. You should know that going in, even if you haven’t read Sunrise on the Reaping. When we first met the character in The Hunger Games, he was Katniss and Peeta’s mentor because he was District 12’s only living victor.

What we didn’t totally know before the release of this book, and subsequent film, was that Haymitch teamed up with other recent victors like Beetee, Mags, and Wiress (as well as future gamemaker Plutarch Heavensbee) to try and take down the games from within. As we first learned that in Catching Fire, the flaws that Haymitch found in the arena contributed to his victory.

President Snow does not like to be beaten and finds creative ways to get revenge against those who double-cross him. We see that early on with Beetee’s son Ampert, who gets reaped to punish Beetee for how he won his games. We see it later with Peeta and Katniss. And Haymitch is allowed to return home at the expense of his mother, brother, and girlfriend. All three die horrifically as soon as he gets back. As many have said: Haymitch didn’t drink enough.

At the end of the film, we see how President Snow’s revenge against Haymitch’s community causes him to spiral fast. With his family and girlfriend dead, in addition to the PTSD from surviving the Hunger Games, he becomes inconsolable and addicted to sleeping syrup. It does not help that he is the only person living in Victor’s Village; because District 12’s only other victor, Lucy Gray Baird, went missing 40 years prior.

One day, Plutarch comes to visit Haymitch ahead of his victory tour to film an update for the Capitol News, and they have a chat. (In the book, this conversation happens during the tour.) He wants Haymitch to keep working with them to overthrow the Capitol. He refuses. “I am living proof the Capitol always wins,” Haymitch says. “You need someone different from me.”

Plutarch insists that they need someone exactly like him, actually. Even if it takes generations and they don’t get to see the results, they have to keep imagining a different future so that one day it comes true. It doesn’t make them heroes. It doesn’t even make them good people. But they’re trying.

Haymitch drifts away from two of his only friends, Burdock Everdeen and Asterid March. If you couldn’t tell from their names, or didn’t hear what they call their infant daughter, yes! Those are Katniss’ parents. (Also, yes! Burdock Everdeen is a member of the Covey. That’s why he sings one of Lucy Gray’s songs, "The Old Therebefore," at the funeral for District 12’s tributes. One day, he’ll change the course of history by teaching her “The Hanging Tree.”

The main reason that Haymitch cuts himself off is grief and guilt. He wants to be alone with his pain. Losing the people he was closest too makes him feel like he doesn’t deserve to be close to anyone, and maybe shouldn’t for their own protection. Movie protagonists are always thinking that, aren’t they? Like, okay Spider-Man! Whatever you say!

But the book reveals another, even more devastating reason: when baby Katniss grows up and starts wearing her hair in pigtail braids, she looks just like Haymitch’s “sweetheart” and first ally, Louella.

As we know from reading and watching The Hunger Games, the rebellion in Panem did eventually find the right victors to raise an army and end the games for good in District 12’s own Peeta Mellark and Katniss Everdeen. They were able to finally implement the plans that Beetee, Wiress, and the other victors had been testing since the second Quarter Quell, if not before.

Without even knowing it, Peeta and Katniss helped Haymitch keep his promise to Lenore Dove. So, of course, the story has to end with them. We see Haymitch, again played by Woody Harrelson, finally celebrating his birthday with no reapings. In Collin’s novel, Haymitch tells Katniss and Peeta about Lenore Dove in order to add her to a District 12 book of memories they’re putting together. Katniss gifts him goose eggs to hatch and raise. The film, however, takes a simpler approach, and just shows old man Haymitch greeting his former mentees before going to spend some alone time with the geese. He’s finally earned some peace.

#6802. Enterprise AI Spending Outpaces Adoption Growth, Report Finds

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a new Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

The report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

"Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

Menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

For enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

John K. Waters is the editor in chief of a number of Converge360.com sites, with a focus on high-end development, AI and future tech. He's been writing about cutting-edge technologies and culture of Silicon Valley for more than two decades, and he's written more than a dozen books. He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS.  He can be reached at [email protected].

#6799. Are We in a Sugar Baby Economy?

Dating is expensive, so why not get paid for it?

Ana, 37, has a rule: she doesn't spend her own money on men. Not on dinner, not on an Uber home, and definitely not on any emotional labor of a situationship that she knows isn’t going to go anywhere. She’s had this rule for three years now.

“I realized over the years that dating men came with a lot of risk,” she tells Cosmopolitan. Ana is bisexual, and she says she kept running into the same thing with men that she never felt with women: a lack of transparency, and the creeping sense of being used.

“At the end of the day, it seemed like the majority of the men I had dated wanted an embellished sex worker, who also provided care and mothering, without necessarily providing something equivalent back.” So she decided to make sure she was getting something back. “Because money, I can count,” she says. “Fake promises? Not really.”

Dating in 2026 is already an expensive extra-curricular on its own. BMO's research puts the average Gen Z date at around $205 once you add up the outfit, the ride, and the actual dinner (millennials clock in even higher, at $252). The average all-in cost of a date climbed 12.5 percent to $189, outpacing the cost of living itself. Bank of America found that more than half of Gen Z, 53 percent of men and 54 percent of women, spend literally $0 a month on dating—because they’re just not doing it.

But even when people are willing to pay the price, it’s hard to find someone to splurge on. Dating app sessions dropped 7 percent year over year in 2025. Swiping is tiring, and paying for premium tiers to keep seeing the same guy you’ve swiped left on on four other apps doesn’t seem worth it. So when “sugar baby” discourse started taking over TikTok and the timeline, it wasn't random.

Clu, 29, remembers exactly how it started. She was working a day job, hustling for what seemed like every dollar, and watching friends who were sugar babies get everything paid for.

“It started off as a financial pressure,” she says. “I'm looking around, I'm seeing these girls get everything paid for, and a lot of my friends are also sugar babies. They're like, ‘Girl, just do it.’”

The tipping point was dating guys her own age and not getting the same treatment. Men who were older and financially stable, on the other hand, knew exactly what they wanted—and were willing to pay for it.

What she's selling is mostly time. “It's really just companionship,” she says, “Going on dates and pretending, most of the time.” Some men want a hand to hold at a lake after a rough day at work while others want a full-on girlfriend experience and promise to cover everything from her bills to a new car. The pay varies wildly: a couple hundred dollars for a date, or, if you get lucky, a designer bag. Twice, Clu says, married men have told her their wives knew and had given their blessing, because they couldn't give their husbands what they were looking for.

“You always want to think of it as a financial transaction because this is a service,” she says. “I'm providing you a service of having a good time and escaping from your reality." Catch feelings, she warns, and things crumble. And never let yourself believe you're the prize: "There's always someone younger. There's always gonna be another sugar baby."

And at first, Clu says the money felt like freedom, but eventually that feeling faded.

“After a while, it does take a toll, because you're constantly depending on these people,” she says. “They can stop paying your bills tomorrow. So it does become financial survival.”

A 2024 study of 77 people in the U.S. and Canada found that money was the primary driver for sugar babies, but companionship mattered to everyone involved, and plenty of arrangements looked a lot like regular dating. It also found that more than a third of the sugar babies had done other kinds of transactional sex work, and that they worried about physical safety and coercion, especially early on.

Sugar dating itself isn't illegal in most places, according to legal explainers on the subject. The line tends to come down to whether money is being exchanged specifically for sex. Which is exactly why so many arrangements stay carefully, deliberately vague.

Ana's current setup doesn't fit the stereotype at all. There's no monthly allowance. Her partner covers things like groceries and Ubers and generally makes her life easier. They live separately and see each other once a week: date night on Saturday, an overnight, brunch on Sunday. They text daily. They aren't exclusive. And all of it was spelled out from the start. “Those were the conditions I set,” she says. “I no longer engage with men without some kind of arrangement being set from the start.”

Before this, she had two more traditional sugar-daddy relationships, which worked more like pay-per-meet. Roughly twice a month, she'd ask for a specific bill to be paid: a shopping spree, repairs at her house, a doctor's bill. She has never liked the idea of a monthly allowance, she explains, because she worried it would make her feel obligated to see people even when she didn't want to.

That autonomy is the point. Ana doesn't frame this as freedom (”I already had that before,” she says) so much as respect. “I have never been treated this nice by men whom I gave my time and love and care for free, so that says a lot.”

“All relationship types come with compromises. But most relationships between men and women come with sometimes feeling pressured to do stuff. And I have learned not to bow.”

But Ana says the sites themselves have changed. "Most sugar arrangement sites have become a place for medium income men to underpay for sex work," she says. In her experience, a lot of them aren't looking for anything complex. “They do want sex by the hour but say they don't want to use escorts as they feel bad about themselves.”

James Foley, LCSW-R, a psychotherapist, treats men who engage in what he calls sugaring behaviors, and he says the economy and the internet both play a role. He explains that social media has given everyone a 24/7, high-resolution view of the rich: their cars, homes, and vacations. Technology, meanwhile, lets people at opposite ends of the economic spectrum connect discreetly and make deals.

But both people—sugar daddies and babies alike–—are walking into an emotionally powerful situation they sometimes can't manage.

“It is a tremendous struggle to maintain your reality testing when something is real and fake at the same time,” he says.

“If you come across the opportunity, why not take it?" Clu says. “Go on that date and come back with that Cartier.” She encourages women to take the chance, as long as they build real relationships instead of treating each man as a one-time payout.

Ana, on the other hand, isn't going back to traditional dating in any form.

In 2026, a lot of people feel like they're paying more and getting less, for dinner, for rent, for love. Sugar dating promises to flip that equation, whether it actually does depends on the contract, the person across the table, and how long you can keep the line between transaction and relationship from blurring.

As Clu puts it, you can be confident in what these men will do for you, and still know the balance can change overnight. Anyone considering it should go in knowing that.

#6798. Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing users to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

The company also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a new model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

Avantis Education, the creator of ClassVR, has introduced two new immersive learning libraries for its Eduverse+ platform: EscapeRooms, a math suite for K-8 students, and LingoLab, a Spanish and English language learning suite for students in grades 6-12.

As schools become more dependent on digital platforms for instruction, grading, student services, and family communication, resilience depends not only on preventing attacks, but on how quickly leaders can restore trusted data, recover essential services, and keep disruptions from cascading across the school community.

#6797. Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Jill Biden Come Together at Gloria Steinem’s Joyous Celebration of Life

The former first ladies coordinated in elegant, high-fashion ensembles to honor the feminist activist

Gloria Steinem’s life, work, and legacy were celebrated this week, as many gathered at a memorial service for the feminist activist in New York City.

The celebration of life took place at the Park Avenue Armory and came two months after Steinem’s passing at age 92.

Among those who came together to pay their respects were former United States first ladies Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Jill Biden—as well as Chelsea Clinton, Diane von Furstenberg, Meg Ryan, Lucy Liu, Emma Watson, Marisa Tomei, and Mariska Hargitay. In total, there were about 1,000 invited guests, all who were encouraged to donate to Gloria’s Foundation, which aims to preserve Steinem’s Upper East Side brownstone on East 73rd Street as a permanent archive and center for feminist organizing.

Rather than a somber service, the memorial was a joyful, music-filled celebration titled “It’s Steinemite!” Cynthia Erivo sang John Lennon’s “Imagine,” Cyndi Lauper performed “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” and Kathy Sledge of Sister Sledge closed the event with “We Are Family,” joined by Lauper and Gloria’s Choir.

For the evening, attendees coordinated in all-black ensembles—but it certainly wasn’t your average funeral attire. Clinton wore an elegant pantsuit—one of her favored looks. Obama was so chic and cool in a cropped blazer and a pleated skirt with a silky sash and golden accents. And Biden went for a fun, high-fashion ensemble that included Schiaparelli’s black Corsini suit jacket with asymmetric gold buttons.

If she could’ve looked into that crowd of incredible women, Steinem would’ve been endlessly proud.

#6790. 27 Charming Christmas Towns That Look Like a Real-Life Holiday Movie

Think twinkling lights, towering trees, and Santa-themed bike rides.

The holiday season is in full swing, with many halls and houses already decked to impress in garland and fairy lights. But as you wrap gifts, prepare to host, and begin marathoning holiday movies, it can feel like the joyous season is coming to an end much too soon. We can't blame you if you're still wanting more from this merry time of year, and we've come up with a solution. There are plenty of beautiful Christmas towns across the country to fill your heart with peace, joy, and nostalgia—you just have to know where to look.

These towns are more than just beautifully decorated—they’re truly immersive, offering experiences from Santa-themed bike rides to orchestrated light shows and winter bar crawls. Below, we've rounded up the 27 most charming Christmas towns from all over the country, so no matter where you live, you'll be close enough to find a bit of extra cheer this year.

This picturesque mountain town serves as the perfect holiday backdrop for more reasons than just the ever-present blanket of fluffy white snow. Each year, the valley is transformed into a Christmas town with seasonal theatrical performances, Gunnison’s Night of Lights, a tree lighting ceremony, and even an ice sculpting event.

Ever since the formation of this city on Christmas Eve in 1741, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, has been rooted in the holiday spirit. From Christmas markets to historical tours to horse-drawn carriage rides, there's no doubt this town won't feel magical. And make sure to stop by the historic Sayre Mansion, pictured here, to check out their elegant holiday decor.

Annapolis is known as one of the best cities during the holiday season thanks to its winter weather and historic downtown. If you're lucky enough to visit this Christmas town, make sure you spend time bargain shopping until midnight, checking out the spectacular light display in Sandy Point State Park, and viewing the Yacht Club Light Parade.

Chicago is exceptionally beautiful during the Christmas time. From the seemingly endless strings of lights to the Christkindlmarket, which is free to enter and so charming, the Windy City has many offerings during the holiday season, making it one of the best Christmas towns to visit. Plus, you don't want to miss ice skating or any Christmas-themed museum exhibits.

If you want to do something Christmas-y almost every single day of December, then Newport, Rhode Island, might just be the place to go. To create the perfect coastal Christmas, this town offers a month-long celebration that's been going strong for 54 years. From holiday bike rides to Medieval festivals to winter afternoon teas, there's so much to do in this Christmas town.

You'll feel as if you've traveled back to Charles Dickens's time when you walk through Franklin's historic Christmas festival. Characters from A Christmas Carol and Oliver Twist come to life throughout the weekend-long festivities. Roam the Victorian Village and try Victorian-era Christmas treats like sugar plums while listening to carolers.

A classic ski town, Park City offers Christmas markets, festive decorations, and a Christmas Eve parade lit by torches—plus spectacular views of the mountains are around every corner.

In the heart of Virginia horse country, you'll find one of the most festive Christmas towns. Cheer on the town's hunting hounds while sipping hard cider and wander the streets in search of vintage Christmas ornaments.

During Kennebunkport's annual Christmas Prelude, the town puts on a very New England celebration: You can watch Santa Claus arrive by lobster boat, go on seashore holiday trolley rides, and enjoy wine tastings and lobster bakes. Not to mention, the town is covered in Christmas lights and garlands that make it the perfect festive photo backdrop.

For a dreamy and unique experience, head to Santa Fe. One of the most anticipated celebrations is the Canyon Road Farolito Walk, which is when thousands of farolitos—luminaries made of paper bags, sand, and tea candles—cast a glow on the gardens and old buildings that line the road. You also can get your white Christmas fix by visiting Ski Santa Fe.

As one of the oldest towns in the country, Portsmouth is a charming New England destination that celebrates the holidays with a Vintage Christmas Celebration. Visit the historic village of Strawberry Banke or wander around the charming shopping districts in this historic Christmas town.

Get a Hallmark movie feel while experiencing a taste of Denmark in California's Solvang village, located in Santa Ynez Valley wine country. The destination hosts Julefest, a month-long holiday celebration with live entertainment, a parade, and a night market.

Koziar's Christmas Village in Bernville is one of the top attractions in Pennsylvania. With more than a million lights adorning buildings, barns, and the landscape—and a reflective lake that doubles the beauty—it's hard to beat the town's display.

This Bavarian-style village is charming any time of year! December festivities include a display of Santa costumes from all around the world, a gingerbread house competition, carolers, and plenty of photo ops.

Of course, New York City isn't a small Christmas town, but it is extra magical during the holidays. From the massive tree at Rockefeller Center to the various Christmas markets in the city parks with ice skating, shops, and more, you can't beat the Big Apple's holiday spirit.

Nicknamed the Lighted Poinsettia Capital of Texas, this town brings major holiday spirit every year. Visit during December when the lighted trail in Comanche Trail Park is aglow all month long. Check out Hotel Settles for its elegant Art Deco lodging.

During the holiday season, each home in Historic Williamsburg lights one candle, a tradition that dates back to the Revolutionary War era. The cobblestone streets and colonial holiday traditions such as caroling by torchlight make this destination a must, especially for history buffs.

This Christmas town stays decked out year-round, so if you're craving holiday spirit in July, you'll still find candy-cane posts, boughs of holly, and a Santa Claus house with live reindeer!

Christmas without the cold? We've got you covered! In addition to abundant sunshine and festive holiday decor, you'll also have plenty of history to explore in St. Augustine, America's oldest city.

Want to take a ride on the Polar Express? Visit Durango during the holidays. The historic mining town offers a Polar Express–inspired trip that your kiddos will flip over.

Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

Meghan Shouse is House Beautiful's Digital Editor, and she's been with the team since September 2023. On top of being the magazine's go-to Waco expert, Meghan also touches on quite a few other verticals in the digital space, like hot news content featuring your favorite HGTV stars, home design inspiration, and the latest interior TikTok trends. However, her favorite pieces are the ones that start conversations, such as stories about resale value and whether or not the Solo cup is chic. Before becoming a home writer, Meghan worked in the fashion industry for two years, writing for Harper's Bazaar after graduating from Iowa State University with a bachelor's degree in apparel merchandising. When she's not interviewing interior designers about home trends, you can find Meghan reading a fictional thriller with her cat in her lap, planning themed parties, or strolling through flea markets searching for chunky candle holders and vintage bookends.

#6788. Ezra Frech and Connor Wood Are the Final Boys

The last two men standing on DWTS talk beating expectations, blocking out the noise, and what happens to their bromance after the ballroom.

One of the best things to come out of Dancing With the Stars season 35? After Guillermo Rodriguez’s assisted knee walks and the chaotic Cat in the Hat dance routine following Tyler Cameron’s baby gender reveal, it’s got to be Ezra Frech and Connor Wood’s unexpected bromance.

Despite premiering over 21 years ago, the show is currently experiencing a major modern resurgence, and social media engagement is to thank. The show has tapped into younger audiences both with its casting choices and through daily behind-the-scenes clips, to the point where even A-listers like Jennifer Lawrence can recognize Connor drinking a smoothie on the street. (By the way, if you’re wondering whether J. Law has reached out to him since he paid her no mind, the answer is sadly no. “I beat that horse to death,” Connor says. “I’m sure she’s like, ‘Can this guy let it go?’”)

And it’s also thanks to social media that fans have gotten a front-row seat to Connor and Ezra’s off-camera bond. What began with a TikTok poking fun at the fact that Connor’s nickname is Fibula and Ezra was born without his left fibula (which was all Ezra’s idea, according to Connor) has blossomed into an iconic friendship. Now, the besties must face off as the two remaining male stars heading into the finale—but they’re not going to let a little competition come between them.

“Ezra is definitely more competitive,” Connor, who’s paired with Rylee Arnold, tells Cosmopolitan. “He’s got a fighting spirit. When we get to eliminations, I’m thinking about my post-show quesadilla. I mean, obviously I want to stay in the competition. But I’ve considered every week that I’ve made it a win. The only person I’m competitive with is myself because I want to get this right.”

“This is a competition show, but you’re kind of rooting for everybody else and want everyone else to do well,” Ezra, who’s partnered with Daniella Karagach, adds. “Plus, there’s so much that’s out of your control. I want Connor to succeed. He wants me to succeed. You know, it’s real love.”

The first time the two met was at the promo photo shoot ahead of the season premiere, where the connection was so instantaneous that Connor thought they must already know each other. As Connor explains, “We’re hugging, we’re chatting, and then I’m walking away like, ‘Oh my gosh, where did I meet him before?’ Turns out, it was our first time meeting. We just connected straight off the bat.”

“Sometimes you’ll meet somebody and just click and know like, ‘Oh, that’s somebody I’m gonna be friends with,’” says Ezra of that fateful first meeting. “I’m sure Connor and I would have definitely hit it off and become really close in any other context—but I think Dancing With the Stars accelerated that timeline because we’re both way out of our comfort zone. For us to be in this together, it’s bonded us in a very unique way.”

They may be a decade apart in age (Connor is 31 as of September, while Ezra was born a month before DWTS first premiered in 2005) and come from two entirely different worlds (Connor is a podcaster and comedian, while Ezra is a two-time Paralympian with two gold medals to prove it), but their friendship? From post-rehearsal dance parties to spray tan dates to trailer talks, it knows no bounds.

Cosmopolitan caught up with Ezra and Connor ahead of the DWTS season 35 finale to chat about beating the odds, blocking out the noise, and what happens after they leave the ballroom.

Connor: I thought there was more to the sentence. I thought I would hear, “Connor and Rylee, come down here and dance for us again.” I literally walked backstage after they called mine and Rylee’s name, and I took off my jacket and just sat on the ground. I was in shock.

Ezra: They do say names are called in no particular order, but when I was standing there with Harry [Shum Jr.], I was just like, “Wow, this is crazy.” No one will tell you that they’re standing up there feeling confident, so when they leave you up there longer, it definitely makes you sweat.

Connor: I’m an extrovert, but it’s very selective. I don’t do emotions. Being on the show, I’ve put out a more vulnerable me. I’ve been sharing things on national TV that I don’t even share with my friends, and it’s been wildly uncomfortable in the best way. You know, I’ve always found work for myself that’s come really easy to me—like, comedy has been natural for me. This is nothing like that. This is the hardest I’ve ever worked in my life, and my brain chemistry has been changed forever because of this.

Ezra: I didn’t come in with any dance experience, and quite frankly, I thought I had natural limitations on what I was capable of on the dance floor. What Dani has brought out of me is almost rewiring the limitations I placed on myself and changing my own expectations of what I can do on a prosthetic—which is crazy, because I’ve lived 21 years and felt like I had a pretty good understanding of what I was capable of on my own prosthetic leg. Then I come on Dancing With the Stars and meet Dani and that completely shifts.

Connor: [laughs] You think I’m watching myself? Oh, no. I don’t watch. And the choreo has been hard, but it’s gotten easier each week for me to learn dances. Like, learning the week 3 samba, I’m like, “Rylee, pack your bags. It’s been great getting to know you.” But now I know that I’ll get it.

Ezra: Yeah, I don’t really watch. I mean, I end up seeing clips, and earlier in the season, I would rewatch the dances. But everything’s happening so fast; it’s hard to, like, really sit and marinate on them when you gotta refocus for the next week. The cool thing is these dances will live forever. They’re out there in the world, and I will be able to watch and appreciate those moments and have pride in them for the rest of my life.

Connor: Michael Scott said it best: “Do I need to be liked? Absolutely not. I like to be liked. I enjoy being liked. I have to be liked.” I relate to that so much, because I’ll want to reach out to someone and be like, “Do you really hate me? Like, walk me through what I did during my jive that has made you just despise me?” I don’t think these people actually have that much hatred in their heart. I think they’re really invested fans, and it’s part of the game. Would I slide into someone’s DMs and say, “Watch your back”? No. But I know it’s what I signed up for.

Ezra: People online—as far as whether they think you’re great or mediocre or suck or whatever the opinions are on social media—shouldn’t influence your day-to-day. Thankfully, for Dani and I, there haven’t been too many negative comments, but, of course, with every 30 positive comments, you’re going to get a negative comment. It’s all about not letting that little negative comment overshadow the beautiful stuff that people are saying online as well.

Connor: This is a once-in-a-lifetime chance, but it’s also objectively fun. It’s a show about dancing. I’m not going to make a joke of it, but there’s humor involved. It’s so important to take a step back and laugh sometimes. This is fun. It should be fun.

Connor: You do it anxious. You know, there are people like Ezra with serious uphill battles, and he’s crushing it. I’m just here with anxiety and ADHD and small amounts of OCD and dancing on TV. It’s just something that I’ve always dealt with. I go into standup anxious, and honestly, I think it helps me operate. It pushes me to make sure I get in all of my rehearsal hours so that there’s nothing to be anxious about. As my dad told me, “If you weren’t anxious, you would be anxious.”

Ezra: I think the way we phrase things in our head controls the way we feel about them. Yes, it can be a burden to feel like you’re representing a community, but it’s a beautiful burden, and so I don’t see it as a negative thing. I get to play a small role in representing my community on such a special show like Dancing With the Stars—I think it’s actually, like, the pride and joy and honor of my life.

Ezra: No, it’s not in my DNA to chill. I mean, after 2028, I’ll probably take some downtime for sure—but then, you know, you’ve got the next Games in 2032, you’ve got world championships the next year, so there’s never really an end. I’ll probably compete on the track for another 15 years or so. And hopefully after the show ends, I’ll take a nice vacation or just rot for a little bit.

Connor: Rylee and Ezra are the same age, and you know, I do feel my age a lot of the time when I talk to them. Like, Rylee only knew who Nicole Kidman was because of the AMC pre-roll ads, and Ezra hadn’t seen High School Musical when we were doing the Wildcats dance. But both of them are so wise beyond their years. As soon as Ezra and I became friends, I started seeing old clips of him at, like, 9 years old on Ellen, and he was probably more eloquent and emotionally mature than I am now. People keep wanting him to be the Bachelor, but I think he needs to run for office. He’s just got this natural charisma.

Ezra: I didn’t listen to his podcast, but I’d seen clips of him online, and I knew of him. There’s a really funny video of a Team USA thing that I did two or three years ago where I’m lip-syncing to Connor’s audio. It’s like, “I have purse; I have shoe.” And now people are like, “Wow, the invisible string theory brought them together.” It’s funny; he’s the exact same online versus in person. He’s the same dude. He’s able to take things in, he’s able to feel them, and then he’s able to articulate them in a way that resonates with people. That’s what makes him so good as a comedian.

Connor: There’s this guy in a suit that’s jumping straight up in the air and it looks like an exclamation point. I’d say that’s Ezra, since he’s so elevated in the way he carries himself. And, of course, he’s got hops.

Ezra: I would describe Connor with the emoji that’s smiling and sweating, because he’s always smiling and he’s always kind of sweating, and it’s sort of perfect. Like, he’ll make jokes and then look around like, “Ooh, did that land?”

Connor: Val [Chmerkovskiy] and Jenna [Johnson] and I are gonna work on hip-hop dance at their studio. Val and I are also doing a standup show together at some point. I just adore Brandon [Armstrong] and Alan [Bersten], too. Us three together? Trouble. Britt [Stewart] and I connected on some zen woo-woo stuff, so we’re gonna hang out. And Jenna Dewan and her partner Steve [Kazee], we’re gonna hang out. Julianne [Hough] and I are gonna hang out in New York. I mean, I talk to everybody. I hope I see everybody again.

Ezra: Amber [Glenn] is someone who is a real close part of my life and will be for a long time. I feel like her and I are on the same team together in this with Pasha [Pashkov] and Dani. Guillermo is someone I’m going to be close to forever. Like me, him, and Connor—we’re in the group chat texting all the time. And I love Tyler Cameron, and Harry is the sweetest, and Jenna—like, it’s hard to pick and choose. I could see myself still talking to pretty much everybody on the cast.

Ezra: The internet is crazy. Right now, I’m definitely single but not necessarily looking for a relationship. Because, again, once the dance season ends, I’ll be committing myself entirely to track again. I’m enjoying being single, and it’ll probably stay that way for a while.

Connor: This has been like a study abroad trip. Like, I am fully immersed in a culture that is so far outside of my comfort zone and so far away from what I know. Learning something new at my age is so rare, let alone at this level on TV with a world-class athlete teaching me. And if it does happen, it probably happens to billionaires’ kids who are, like, paying Serena Williams to do private lessons for two years. I think I’m gonna wake up on Wednesday feeling like I walked out of a loud party and shut the door with my ears still ringing. Like, I’m alone. Party is over. It’s time to go home.

Ezra: I’ll miss getting to see everyone at the rehearsal studio. I’ll miss getting lunch with Dani after practice. I’ll miss getting the opportunity to commit myself to something like this so entirely. And I’m gonna miss the show days. You become so close to everybody, and you spend so much time around these people, and then all of a sudden, it’s going to end. But the good thing is that these people are still going to be in my life. I’m still going to hang out with Dani, and I’m still going to see Connor whenever I can, and we’ll get lunch with Guillermo. These are people I’ll be with forever.

#6787. Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Miley Cyrus can buy herself flowers, but we have a feeling that her beau, Maxx Morando, is buying them for her.

Since 2021, the Disney Channel alum has been linked to Morando, a fellow musician who is perhaps best known as being the drummer for the rock band Liily. He was also previously part of another group, called the Regrettes. In 2022, Lilly was invited to play on Cyrus’s TV special, Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party.

Throughout their years-long relationship, the two have preferred to keep their romance largely out of the spotlight. But Cyrus offered a rare glimpse into their life together during her interview for the Harper’s Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story. “He’s very similar to me,” she said. “We just don’t take life too seriously.”

Throughout their time together, they’ve also collaborated numerous times in the studio, with Morando serving as a producer and songwriter on Cyrus’s Something Beautiful and Bass Persuades records. In her interview with Bazaar, Cyrus revealed that music was actually how she and Morando first got to know each other. “I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus said. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

Now, the pair are engaged and reported to be getting married this weekend with an intimate ceremony in Southern California. However, other details are being kept under wraps—for now.

If you’re wondering what else there is to know about Cyrus and Morando’s low-key romance, then look no further. Below, we’ve tracked the couple’s entire relationship from start to finish.

For Cyrus, it was love at first sight, but for Morando, he already had an idea of who he was meeting long before the date even happened.

“We got put on a blind date,” Cyrus reveals in an interview with British Vogue years after the fact, in May 2023. “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’ ”

When he calls mid-interview, her phone starts playing “Tyrone” by Erykah Badu. “I call that ‘boyfriend sexy ringtone,’ ” she says, smiling.

In an interview with Vogue, Cyrus discusses the outfits that she wore for her sets at Summerfest in Milwaukee and Atlanta’s Music Midtown festival. Turns out, one of the pieces—a faux-leather set crafted by Shane Kastl—includes cartoon monsters sketched by Morando.

During the interview, Cyrus comments on the custom design, saying, “This look is a one-of-a-kind collaboration between two of my favorite emerging artists, Maxx Morando and Shane Kastl. Shane used existing pieces I’ve collected over time and customized Maxx’s cartoon characters [within] his construction. Their collaboration is the perfect example of sustainability becoming the next fashion phase, and it proves that anything can be reinvented, which resonates with me deeply.”

The pair spark dating rumors when they make their first public appearance at the Gucci Love Parade fashion show in November.

For the event, Cyrus wears a metallic blue fringe dress with a contrasting cream feather drop waist, which she pairs with strappy golden sandals. Meanwhile, Morando sports a burgundy suit over a G-logo top, with white sneakers featuring the signature Gucci red and green stripes.

Shortly after the event, Cyrus shares a slideshow where the third photo sees her and Morando posing together on the red carpet. In her caption, the singer writes, “LOVE PARADE ❤️💕 @gucci @alessandro_michele.”

A fan captures a sweet video of Morando supporting Cyrus backstage for her NBC holiday special, Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party. In the clip, the two can be seen smiling and dancing together.

Days later, paparazzi snap photos of the two enjoying a vacation together in Miami, where the special was filmed.

Cyrus and Morando make a rare joint appearance together for Versace’s Fall/Winter 2023 fashion show in West Hollywood.

Later in the day, the two attend the launch party for Cyrus’s eighth studio album, Endless Summer Vacation, in Beverly Hills. Paparazzi photos—which you can see here—show Cyrus dressed to the nines in a sparkly black one-shoulder minidress and a vibrant green fur jacket. Morando looks equally stylish in a navy-blue velvet suit.

A source tells People where Cyrus’s head is at amid her relationship with Morando.

“She’s the healthiest and happiest she’s been in a long time,” the source says, then goes on to describe how Cyrus has healed following her 2020 divorce from Liam Hemsworth: “Everyone was blaming her for the divorce and calling her this wild child, but that wasn’t fair. Their relationship and marriage was toxic, and she was heartbroken.”

A second insider tells the outlet that Morando is a “cool guy.”

“He has no interest in being a huge celebrity; he’s very low-key. Miley loves these qualities,” the source explains. “Miley can be herself. They are supportive of each other’s careers. Miley is enjoying life and things are great.”

Morando supports Cyrus at the 66th-annual Grammy Awards ceremony, where the singer wins her first-ever golden gramophone.

During the ceremony, the couple is joined by Cyrus’s family members, mom Tish Cyrus and sister Brandi Cyrus.

A source for People opens up about Cyrus and Morando’s joyful home life together.

“She is very happy with him,” the insider claims. “Miley has changed a lot in the past couple of years. She seems more calm and harmonious. Everyone loves Maxx. He’s a great guy. She is very happy with him. He’s private and doesn’t like being in the press. It’s been good for her.”

In a new Dolce & Gabbana campaign video, Cyrus poses in a sultry all-black look and shares the song “Imitate,” a track from Morando’s band, Liily.

Cyrus offers rare details on her love story with Morando in an interview for Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story.

“He’s very similar to me. We just don’t take life too seriously,” she says.

While the two have a small age gap—Cyrus is six years Morando’s senior—she reflects on how their different upbringings have made them approach life differently.

“He looks at life really differently than I do,” she explains. “He grew up with a laptop. I had a desktop computer that I shared with my brothers and sisters. … Honestly, he’s raised our dog off Reddit. I’m like, Are you sure we’re supposed to be doing this? And he’s like, On Reddit it says blah, blah, blah.”

She also opens up about working with Morando on musical projects and how collaboration is her love language. “I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other. I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus says. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

Morando and Cyrus are photographed behind-the-scenes at the 67th Grammy Awards, where Cyrus snags her third Grammy for her collaboration on Beyoncé’s “II Most Wanted.” The appearance marks a rare joint public outing by the couple, who match in all-black ensembles.

Morando wears his usual red-carpet uniform to stand by his partner at the 97th Academy Awards. Cyrus wears a black gown with a distressed bodice embellished with sequins, which she wears with a curly hairdo and bleached brows.

Cyrus and Morando walk the red carpet for the Hollywood premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash, and there, the singer debuts a chunky gold ring with a large, square diamond at the center.

Hours later, People confirms the two are engaged.

The engaged pair wear cool all-black looks to the show and look so in love as they embrace at their star-studded table during the ceremony.

Cyrus is sleek in a moto-inspired fit from Celine, while Morando goes low-key in a black T-shirt and pants.

Following their engagement news, a source tells People that the couple wants a “smaller and meaningful” wedding rather than a “huge, traditional” event.

“Maxx is extremely private, and that’s just not who he is,” the source says. “When they do get married, it will be something smaller and meaningful to them. Not a big Hollywood production.”

While it’s unclear when the Hannah Montana singer plans to wed her drummer fiancé, the source says Cyrus is enjoying this era and her engagement: “Miley really loves her life right now. Everything just feels like it’s falling into place for her.”

At the world premiere of the Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special in Los Angeles, Cyrus walks the red carpet alongside her fiancé.

For the occasion, the Disney Channel alum wears a plunging silver Rabanne dress layered over a bedazzled Hannah Montana tee, while her beau opts for a white tee and black jeans, which he pairs with black-and-white sneakers from Celine.

Cyrus is honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, thanks to her “lasting impact on the entertainment industry.” In reference to Cyrus’s work on Hannah Montana and more, Walk of Fame producer Ana Martinez notes: “Generations of young girls have grown up watching her evolve, finding inspiration in her journey and fearless creativity.”

At the ceremony, Cyrus is supported by members of her family like mom Tish and her older half-sister, Brandi. Meanwhile, Morando shows his support too, posing with Cyrus in front of the plaque.

Nearly a year after the pair reveal their engagement, TMZ reports that they will tie the knot with a secret ceremony in Southern California, scheduled to take place on the weekend of November 20.

Although other details are kept under wraps, Cyrus is seen running errands—like like getting her nails done—ahead of the ceremony.

She seemed to have been teasing the nuptials a month prior, when she brought out Morando during her Hollywood Bowl shows to do a surprise rendition of “Let’s Get Married.”

#6785. Jenna Johnson Called Out “Online Bullying” and “Hate” from ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Fans

“Hate has become so relevant and intertwined with the show.”

It’s been almost a week since Jenna Johnson and Harry Shum Jr.’s shocking elimination from Dancing With the Stars, and now that she’s had some time to process, Jenna says she’s hoping fans of the show can get back to spreading joy instead of online bullying.

“I feel like Dancing with the Stars used to be the show that everyone tuned into to turn off the noise and to just experience two hours of pure joy, and entertainment, and excitement,” she told People. “So it’s sad that this online bullying and hate has become so relevant and intertwined with the show.”

Jenna certainly isn’t the only person on Dancing With the Stars season 35 to speak out about the increasingly negative vibes on social media.

Harry previously told E! News, “I hope they address that at a certain point. Because I think there’s a good amount of bullying that doesn’t feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it.”

Meanwhile, Jenna Dewan told Extra when she was eliminated, “I know it’s hard to know how this all plays into it. I know this was a particularly tough week for a lot of the online noise and all stuff that comes with the show. I don’t know, I’ll never know how, or if, any of that plays into this. But I know that we went out there and had the best time of our life.”

Plenty of shows have had to issue anti-bullying PSAs to their audience ahead of the show (including Love Island and The Summer I Turned Pretty), so it’s possible Dancing With the Stars will follow suit next season.

#6775. Sharna Burgess Calls Out ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Voting System for Letting Fans “Manipulate the Show”

Dancing With the Stars operates on a pretty simple scoring system that pretty much boils down to one part judges and one part audience. But pro Sharna Burgess thinks fans are using their online votes to manipulate the show and vote off talented dancers that shouldn’t be going home.

Speaking on Instagram Stories after Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson were eliminated, Sharna said (per E! News), “The online discourse is so wild that [it] was pretty clear who fans were ‘voting off’ and how they have felt about dance experience contestants.”

“[It’s] so disappointing to see our voting system is now being used by viewers to vote people off instead of voting for your favorite,” she added. “I say we got [sic] back to yall only have 10 votes total and you have to figure out how to dish them out. This voting ppl off thing is so insanely negative and not what we are built on and it’s seemingly given fans the chance to manipulate the show. JMO.”

There’s been a lot of discourse about the Dancing With the Stars voting system in light of Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr. both going home despite delivering flawless routines and getting high judges’ scores. Jenna even alluded to the online discourse playing a role in her elimination, telling Extra, “I know it’s hard to know how this all plays into it. I know this was a particularly tough week for a lot of the online noise and all stuff that comes with the show. I don’t know, I’ll never know how, or if, any of that plays into this. But I know that we went out there and had the best time of our life.”

Dancing With the Stars producers haven’t addressed voting concerns or indicated that they’re making any changes, but stay tuned.

#6774. From the Archive: Ina Garten Tapped a Few Famous Friends for Her '90s Farmhouse Renovation

Take a look inside the sunny, five-room farmhouse.

Welcome to Archive Dive—my new excuse to obsess over the absolute treasures hiding in House Beautiful’s 130-year-old archives. Every month, we’ll dig up a favorite story from the past (epic room makeovers, wildly bold design swings, and style moments that were way ahead of their time) and talk about why they still resonate today. It’s part history lesson, part design deep-dive, and 100 percent a love letter to the iconic taste that’s defined HB for over a century.—Jo Saltz, House Beautiful Editor in Chief

After Ina Garten moved the now-shuttered Barefoot Contessa specialty store from Westhampton to East Hampton, she and her husband, Jeffrey, decided to put down roots in the neighborhood. But rather than buy a new-build home, Garten transformed an old farmhouse into a light-filled, five-room retreat designed for hosting—and feeding—guests.

In our latest Archive Dive, we revisit the 1994 renovation, which includes Garten’s search for the right paint color, her no-nonsense decorating approach, and her love of the property’s grounds. She took each project in stride with help from famous friends like Martha Stewart and the late interior designer Robert Currie—and Jeffrey, of course. The result was a relaxed home with an entertaining-ready atmosphere and a garden that would make any green-thumbed foodie proud. Read on for the original story.

With the help of Robert Currie, the owner of a fabulous food emporium in the Hamptons planned her nearby house for the casual ease of the legions of guests she feeds in her spare time.

Are you full of self-doubt in the dark of the night? Should you buy that old house? Should you change your career? Then follow in Ina Garten’s (bare) footsteps. She has done both with such breathtaking speed and success that the average worrier blinks in awe. She bought a Westhampton, New York, specialty store (oddly shaped breads, ravishing vegetables, seafood salad to go) from a business opportunities ad practically on the spot.

“I didn’t know how to slice smoked salmon or tell whether the Brie was ripe,” she confesses. But in no time, she turned her emporium, Barefoot Contessa, into a foodie’s fairyland.

After Garten moved the store to East Hampton she converted a cramped, run-down old farmhouse in the village into an airy five-room refuge and party venue for herself and her husband. “I just trusted that if the house had good ‘bones,’ I could figure it all out,” she laughs. No insomnia. No agonies. And, incredibly, no mistakes.

She’s a nurturer, too, a definite Earth Mother, which is certainly why she fled her career in nuclear energy policy planning for the far more congenial field of food. Her personal policy is summed up simply: lots of entertaining.

When her husband—a former Columbia professor, author, and investment banker—worked in New York, she encouraged his uptight fellow bankers to loosen their ties and shed their jackets by dishing up platters of fried chicken and other finger foods. In East Hampton she gives Sunday afternoon parties with plenty of easy food “like crabcake sandwiches,” and leaves all the doors open so guests will feel free to wander out and eat on the porch, or anywhere else that seems inviting.

She often serves in her sunny kitchen, which contains the requisite serious fridge and stove, but lacks the usual array of self-important utensils. This is a kitchen with nothing to prove.

The toughest decisions of her fix-up were the wall colors. She thought at first that she might like the whole house vanilla (a true foodie’s choice), but test patches were too white or yellow.

“I had samples all over the walls, and the painter was yelling ‘Stop already’,” but finally she hit on a toasty khaki for her bedroom. She was still stuck for the first floor when she spotted the bedroom primer paint: khaki halved with white. A mental lightbulb turned on, and the painter went to work. The house is now two values of that changeable shade with browny greens in the upholstery derived from the tapestry-covered living room sofa.

There is not a stick of unnecessary furniture in the farmhouse either, just several old oversize tables, a few pieces of portly upholstery, and in the bedroom, a brass bed (of which a friend said, “That’s not a bed, it’s a temple”), plus two chairs. No windows are curtained.

“Everything,” Garten feels, “should do something, have a function, not just sit there. I like things to be spare.” And bare as well, like her new floors, which are crafted of newly purchased old wood. Are the original floors still underneath? Nope. With a sanding and a coat of polyurethane, they are reincarnated as a kitchen countertop.

Garten actually bought the house for its grounds, because she yearned to garden. She had lived for a time in rented houses, but when she found herself planting expensive trees in rented lawns, she realized it was time to own some land.

Outside her kitchen doors she has cut square beds for tomatoes, which mix quite cheerfully with dahlias, and for roses knee-deep in catmint. She likes to combine “mess with structure,” but her structures are always imaginative. Instead of a single stake for each tomato plant, for instance, she does a row of tepees. Or she lines her disheveled strawberry beds with a spine of iris.

A Manhattan florist friend, Tom Pritchard of Pure Mädderlake, helped her with the garden design and did a very clever thing. He took two chairs out into the garden and walked around with her, scoping out the best seating spots. That’s how she decided which vistas to emphasize and which had too fine a view of the neighbor’s patio. Gardening has become a passion since she moved here. Every surface in her house is piled with well-thumbed horticultural tomes; for the time being, her food banks are relegated to the bottom of the pile.

Garten acknowledges that she has had a lot of help. Her good friend, the late Robert Currie, designed all the seating, shopped with her, and arranged the furniture. He also taught her to avoid like mad “anything that was too trendy.” Stephen Scanniello, the rose dean at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, chose a hundred great roses for her, and Martha Stewart passed judgment on her new shower stall. No less helpful was her very supportive husband.

But husbands don’t ponder that midnight ceiling with you. And talented friends aren’t around at 2 a.m., when the real bullets are bitten. Some lucky people, though, do it all with ease—Ina Garten for one. Warm and comfy, like her own new house, she just turns over and goes back to sleep.

#6772. Before & After: This Couple Planned to Flip a 62-Year-Old Fixer-Upper, Then Made It Their Home Instead

Designer Claire Thompson and her husband tackled the house together room by room.

Designer Claire Thompson has a theory about renovating a house alongside your significant other: If your relationship can survive that, it can probably survive anything. In 2021, she and her now-husband, Will, purchased a nearly 5,000-square-foot home in Jackson, Mississippi’s Eastover neighborhood, with plans to renovate the property and flip it for a profit. By 2022, they were engaged in the unfinished kitchen. Four years later, they’re still there, now with a baby daughter and a house that looks very little like the one they originally intended to sell.

Built in 1964, the five-bedroom property hadn’t been meaningfully upgraded in decades. The rooms were compartmentalized, the finishes were dated, and the quirky floor plan presented a few head-scratching challenges, like a second-floor dining room entirely removed from the kitchen below. But Thompson, who launched her design business in 2020, saw something worth holding onto. “I quickly fell in love with the bones of the home, the lot the home is positioned on, and of course the neighborhood and the street itself,” she recalls.

The decision to stay rather than sell came with a change in approach. Rather than gutting the house and putting in finishes they knew would grab buyers in a post-COVID market, the couple worked within the home’s existing footprint, opening up walls to encourage better circulation while preserving the individuality of each room. The kitchen, once closed off at either end, now connects to a light-filled breakfast nook and an inviting keeping room, where damaged parquet floors and dated ceiling beams gave way to white oak underfoot and softly textured plaster overhead.

Nearby, a former study became an inky, book-lined library, complete with an expanded bar. Even the upstairs dining room survived, despite its logistical inconveniences. “We decided to keep it because of the way it flows when we entertain and host showers or parties,” Thompson says. “I think a home that tells a story, like a nod to the past or an interesting quirk, only makes the home more intriguing.”

The renovation unfolded after hours, with Will building cabinetry and tackling electrical work late into the night. Some spaces were even renovated twice: first, with resale in mind, then with the more personal considerations of permanence. The home became a testing ground for Thompson’s design practice, but it also serves as something of a family scrapbook. “We grew together as individuals, as a couple, as business owners, and as creatives,” she says. “The home feels like us.”

FAST FACTSDesigner: Claire Thompson DesignLocation: Jackson, MississippiThe Space: A five-bedroom, four-and-a-half-bathroom home across 5,000 square feet.

The kitchen layout didn’t change too much, but Thompson was able to completely upgrade its feel and functionality by opening up both ends—one to the breakfast nook, one to the keeping room—and adding a center island.

“I really did not want upper cabinets in the kitchen, so we were very thoughtful in the functionality of the cabinetry,” she adds. “My husband loves to remind me that he built me 42 drawers for the kitchen. We have ample storage, while still making it aesthetically the way I envisioned.”

Now open to the kitchen, the breakfast nook acts as a natural overflow spot where the family eats most of their meals, casual dinners included. Removing the ceiling beams allowed Thompson to capture the feel of taller ceilings; while she wanted to keep the brick floors, opening up the walls meant she had to opt for new white oak for continuity.

“We call this the keeping room since we opened it up to the kitchen,” explains Thompson. “This is the room we really live in day to day; it’s a laid-back and comfortable space.”

The pair started by plastering just the fireplace, but then decided to extend the treatment throughout the rest of the room—it’s since become a signature finish for Thompson’s firm. “We now use this technique in almost every project,” she adds.

Previously a study, the library was born of equal parts design instincts and necessity. “My husband has so many books that we decided to wrap the room with bookshelves,” explains Thompson, who also reworked a hallway to add a bar and powder bathroom. The whole space is drenched in a Roman clay finish (Black Star by Portola Paints), creating an enveloping retreat that has become a go-to for family movie nights.

Also known as the family’s “Christmas tree room,” the formal living room is a soothing symphony of neutral hues and nubby textures. “The coffee table is one of my favorite purchases of all time,” Thompson adds. “I bought it to sell to a client but decided I couldn’t part with it! I also love to have my grandmother’s antique stool in here—it always makes me think of her and brings me joy.”

Perfectly balanced between sweet and sophisticated, 12-week-old daughter Margot’s bedroom was an opportunity for Thompson to lean into all things childhood magic. “She may never leave the bassinet in our primary bedroom, but she does have a cute room waiting for her if that ever happens!” she adds.

Connected to the nursery through a Jack-and-Jill bathroom, this guest space could eventually become a bedroom for a second child. For now, though, it’s a comfortable spot for visiting guests, and a favorite hideout of Thompson’s “first baby,” pup Lemmon.

Claire Thompson is the owner of Claire Thompson Design, a full-service firm specializing in designing, renovating, and furnishing beautiful, timeless homes. She works closely with clients to ensure their unique personalities and desires are perfectly captured by the design and that all their wishes and needs are met.
