#6770. Where Is Karen Read Now? Netflix’s Latest True Crime Doc Revisits the John O’Keefe Case

A new three-part true crime documentary on Netflix unpacks the case.

Between the Christmas ads on TV and the colder temps that have made our morning commutes ever-so-slightly more unpleasant, it’s safe to say that winter has arrived. That calls for more time spent at home, snuggled up on the sofa with a good true crime series to binge. And speaking of, Netflix has us covered there with its latest release, The Trials of Karen Read.

As the name suggests, Netflix’s newest three-part documentary follows the criminal trial of Karen Read. But who is Karen Read? What was she on trial for? And where is Karen Read now? Here’s everything you need to know...

Karen Read, who lived in Mansfield, Massachusetts, is a former financial analyst and professor of finance at Bentley University.

During COVID-19, she dated police officer John O’Keefe. They had previously been involved romantically, but had rekindled things during the pandemic after he reached out to her on social media. “He had reached out to me on Facebook,” she told Nightline. “He said, ‘Hey, blast from the past. How’s things?’”

John O’Keefe was an officer in the Boston police force, a position he’d held for 14 years.

On the night of January 28, 2022, Read drove O’Keefe to the home of Brian Albert, a retired Boston police officer, as the pair planned to catch up. Read stayed in the car outside Albert’s home for 10 minutes as she waited to find out if she should join the gathering, but when she didn’t hear anything, she drove home. Given the time of year, the weather was pretty wintry, with low temperatures, wind, and a lot of snow.

When O’Keefe didn’t return home, Read and some mutual friends went looking for him. In Albert’s driveway, the search party found O’Keefe unconscious and covered in snow. He was pronounced dead after being taken to a nearby hospital. O’Keefe was 46.

A medical examination carried out after O’Keefe’s death found traumatic injuries, including skull fractures, two black eyes, and blood around his nose and mouth, per CNN. His cause of death was listed as “blunt force trauma to the head and hypothermia,” but it couldn’t be concluded whether his death was accidental or a homicide.

Three days after John O’Keefe’s death, Karen Read was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter (which was later upgraded to second-degree murder), motor vehicle homicide, and leaving the scene of a personal injury or crime. She denied all of the allegations against her and pleaded not guilty.

At court, prosecutors put forth that Read was drunk on the night of the alleged crime. They said she was angry at her partner and intentionally hit him with her SUV. Meanwhile, Read’s defense team argued that she was framed for his death and that law enforcement had conspired to cover up who really killed O'Keefe.

As the trial played out in both court and on social media, many theories were thrown about. Some suggested that Read deliberately hit O'Keefe with her car, while others alleged he was killed by someone else at the Albert home. By that account, O’Keefe’s body was dumped in the front garden where it was hidden in the snow.

Theories aside, neither the prosecution nor the defense succeeded in proving what really happened. In July 2024, the jury told the judge they could not reach a unanimous verdict and, as such, a mistrial was declared.

In June 2025, at her second trial, Read was acquitted of second-degree murder and the two lesser charges against her. Instead, Read was convicted of driving while under the influence and sentenced to one year of probation due to having no previous criminal convictions.

Since her second trial, Read has kept a relatively low profile, but she has not stayed out of the legal system altogether. She sued Massachusetts State Police and the town of Canton for negligence and civil conspiracy, arguing that they were biased in their investigation. Read was later awarded $100,000 by the Massachusetts State Police, which agreed to settle her lawsuit.

#6762. Jennifer Lawrence Slips Into Statement Slippers for an Easy Autumn Walk

She brightened up her porcelain car coat with a pop of red

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping premiere, the Beauty Inc. Awards, a Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon appearance, and more: Jennifer Lawrence has spent much of the past week all glammed up. But on Friday, November 20, during a rare day off, the actor kept things casual—taking a New York City walk in a fall look that reminded us her street style still rivals a red-carpet alternative.

Known for her effortless layering, high-low styling, and hints of leopard prints, Lawrence stepped out in West Village wearing an easy, casual black-and-white ensemble... with a little pop of autumnal red. On top, she wore a plum-purple T-shirt under a porcelain-beige car coat from the Row, crafted from structured cotton and tailored with a long body lined with silk. The outerwear featured a little collar, concealed buttons, and welt pockets—creating a sleek silhouette.

As for trousers, Lawrence opted for casual black track pants with parallel red stripes down each leg. She matched the accent hue to her bold statement slippers: a pair of deep-ruby calf-hair slip-ons perched atop a black platform base. The shoes appeared to be a version of Birkenstock’s classic Boston style, with silver-tone buckle straps across each instep.

For further accessories, the Hunger Games star wore black sunglasses, some Airpods, her go-to gold Sidney Garber necklace, and a small Guidi handbag. The new bag, first spotted on Lawrence’s arm in October, was crafted from black leather with thick rounded straps and shiny silver hardware.

#6760. The Exact Order You Should Apply Your Skincare, According to Dermatologists

Following this routine completely changed our skin for the better.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

The world of skincare can quickly become confusing and overwhelming. Doom-scrolling through SkinTok makes things seem even more complicated. Like, how many steps do you actually need? Which serums are worth using? What products are totally superfluous? If you followed every bit of “foolproof” advice you found on the app, your skin barrier would be compromised and your complexion could look worse than before you went down this rabbit hole.

Well, it’s time to stop mindlessly scrolling and start reading because team Cosmo tapped experts to break down the ideal skincare routine order that’s streamlined and effective for your exact concerns.

Trust us, it's a lot to consider even for beauty editors who spend their entire day testing all of these products, let alone a beginner just trying to get glowy, clear skin or deter fine lines. But step by step, we're gonna make sense of it all, below.

First things first: You do not need a 10-step skincare routine (or even a 5-step routine!). "Less is more when it comes to your skin—I'm all about product reducing," says dermatologist Karan Lal, MD. "In reality, our skin chemistry needs hydration and moisture to maintain a good skin barrier, which you can get from just a few products." And, as virtually all dermatologists agree, those products include the following:

That's it. The three most important skincare products are cleanser, moisturizer, and SPF. It’s not glamorous, but good skin doesn’t need to be (just ask your dermatologist or anyone on the Cosmo beauty team—simple is always better). The more products you layer on, the higher your risk is for irritation, allergic reactions, and breakouts, notes Dr. Lal.

Now, if you're looking to build a slightly more advanced skincare routine, we're totally on board with that, too. Keep reading to learn how to incorporate more skincare steps, and what order they should be applied.

“The rule of thumb when applying skincare is to apply the lightest formula first and the heaviest last since thinner products can’t penetrate thicker products,” says dermatologist Shereene Idriss, MD. Example: Layering a serum (thin) on top of your moisturizer (thick) would render that serum almost ineffective because it can't absorb into your skin when there's an occlusive barrier sitting on top of it.

Please, for the love of the beauty gods, remove your makeup and wash your face before slathering on your skincare products. “For ingredients to absorb properly, you need clean skin that’s totally free of oil and grime,” says dermatologist Mona Gohara, MD, which is where double-cleansing comes in.

Wondering how to double cleanse? The simplest method is to remove your makeup with a cleansing oil or balm (neither is "better" than the other; it's just personal preference). This step will dissolve all the makeup on your face without stripping your skin.

Then, follow that up with a gentle cleanser that works with your skin type. Dry skin should look for creamy, non-foaming face washes with barrier-boosting ingredients like ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and glycerin; while oily skin should try gel-based face washes or gentle foaming cleansers.

Those with acne-prone skin will benefit from a formula with added acne-fighting ingredients, like salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide. Keep in mind, though: If your skin is sensitive, use soothing formulas loaded with things like colloidal oatmeal, aloe vera, and niacinamide.

It depends, but usually yes. If you have oily or acne-prone skin, then definitely yes—cleansing after you wake up is a good way to get rid of any grime or shine that's collected overnight. However, if you have dry or sensitive skin, you probs don't need to re-wash ahead of the rest of your routine, but if you're a sweaty sleeper, it's always a good idea to freshen your face before the rest of your skincare routine.

Face toners used to be terrible, alcohol-based liquids that burned your face. But today’s (good) toners are either filled with gentle, hydrating ingredients for dry and sensitive skin, or filled with chemical exfoliants to treat acne and bumps. “Toners are not meant to be something that sits around on your skin and feels heavy,” says Dr. Gohara. “They’re just priming your face for ingredients to be better absorbed later on.”

Reminder: Toner (like most of the steps on this list) is optional, but if your toner smells like nail polish remover or alcohol, you need to ditch it—fast—and find an updated version instead. The best toner for acne-prone or oily skin is gonna be filled with ingredients that'll help unclog pores and prevent breakouts, like salicylic acid and/or AHAs. Tap it on your skin every other night (or morning, if you plan to use a retinol at night), then wait 60 seconds before layering another product.

If your skin is dry and/or sensitive, choose a toner with hydrating ingredients to reduce potential irritation (like hyaluronic acid, polyglutamic acid, squalane, ceramides, etc.). You can pat this onto your skin every morning, night, or both.

Toners and essences are pretty interchangeable in their consistencies, so if you’re looking for when to use your essence in your skincare routine, use it as step 2 (instead of toner). If you happen to have both in your routine, swipe on a toner first, then pat in an essence. (Think of it like a thin moisturizer-serum hybrid.)

Exfoliators keep skin smooth and clear by removing built-up dead skin cells and excess oil that can dull your complexion and block product absorption. They should be used after toner, when the skin is clean and balanced, and before serums so your treatments can penetrate more effectively.

There are two types of exfoliators: Chemical and physical. Chemical exfoliants use acids or enzymes (like AHAs, BHAs, or PHAs) to dissolve dead skin cells and are best for concerns like acne, clogged pores, uneven texture, and dark spots. Physical exfoliants use gentle scrubbing particles to manually buff skin smooth and can give instant results, but should be used carefully to avoid irritation.

Incorporate an exfoliator into your routine one to three times per week for ongoing skin concerns, especially if you have sensitive or acne-prone skin. Don’t forget to follow exfoliation with hydrating products and sunscreen during the day, too!

“Serums are essentially shots of extremely concentrated nutrients, hydrators, or antioxidants that really amp up your skin health as soon as you apply them,” says Dr. Gohara. “People often skip out on using them, but they’re honestly the heavy lifters of your skincare routine.” So, while serums are totally optional, they’re often a good first step to leveling up your skincare routine and boosting your skin health.

For almost all skin types, Dr. Gohara, Dr. Lal, Dr. Idriss, and every other derm in existence, swear by using a vitamin C serum in the morning, which protects your skin from inflammation and damage caused by environmental factors, while also brightening dark spots over time. Just note: Vitamin C can be strong, so if your skin is sensitive, use it every other morning (or every two mornings) instead.

Though serums are optional, all skin types can benefit from using a hydrating, hyaluronic-acid-based serum at night (and, honestly, in the morning too), which pulls water into your skin from the air to keep it hydrated. “If you’re using acne treatments or anti-aging products—which can be drying or irritating—you want to prep your skin with as much moisture as possible first,” says Dr. Idriss.

Totally. But when it comes to layering serums, keep in mind the thin-to-thick rule, says dermatologist Jessie Cheung, MD. "Thicker serums may impede the absorption of the thinner formulations," she notes. So you'll want to start with your watery, vitamin C serums, then layer on rich, creamy formulas after.

Eye creams tend to be lighter and thinner than face moisturizers, so make sure to apply them before your creams and oils if you opt to use one. (Remember: lighter products go before heavier products).

For morning use, look for an eye cream that's packed with caffeine, which helps temporarily constrict and tighten puffy under-eyes within 20 minutes. And, ideally, opt for one with a cooling applicator; “the cold steel helps with fluid retention—aka under-eye bags—especially if you keep the cream in the fridge between uses,” says Dr. Gohara.

“Most people think a night eye cream should contain retinol to help with fine lines, but in reality, you want to be gentle," says Dr. Gohara. "Your eye area is delicate and at risk for irritation, so tap on a simple, hydrating eye cream that’ll protect your under-eyes and repair your skin barrier overnight.”

Ideally, spot treatments are best applied at night (whether they’re for zits, scars, or dark spots), because that’s when your body is working hardest to repair itself, says Dr. Gohara. But if your nighttime routine already includes acids or retinoids, try spot-treating in the morning, so you don’t irritate your skin with too much at once.

Regardless of when you apply your spot treatment, make sure to tap it on before your moisturizer so it can really penetrate your skin and do the most without having another barrier to penetrate (before?! What?! Yes, just trust the process and keep reading).

For scars: Dr. Idriss recommends using a spot treatment with either hydroquinone (a skin-bleaching ingredient that works fast but can be highly irritating) or niacinamide (aka vitamin B3), which gently brightens marks and scars over time. Niacinamide can be used daily (most formulas won’t cause irritation), but hydroquinone should be used once every three days to be safe (zero irritation after two weeks? Move it up to every other day).

For acne: Dr. Gohara stands by tried-and-true benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid—but not together, unless you want to dry out or irritate your skin. Benzoyl peroxide kills acne-causing bacteria (use it for classic whiteheads), while salicylic acid dissolves oil and skin cells (use it for little clogged pores and inflamed bumps).

How to use spot treatments:Regardless of which formula you choose, the application is the same: Dab a thin layer over your spot or zit and wait a full minute for it to dry. Then, to prevent the treatment from getting wiped around your face, apply your moisturizer to the rest of your face, avoiding the spots. When your face is fully moisturized, tap a dot of moisturizer on top of the spot treatment.

You should stick on a pimple patch (which, FYI, is a sticker that help protect your pimple, soak up any excess fluid or oil around it, and potentially help treat your zit depending on if it has added actives like salicylic acid) before moisturizer, just as you would with other spot treatments. Typically, I will stick on a pimple patch, then carefully spread my moisturizer across my face to avoid moving the patch around.

"You need to be using a moisturizer twice a day," says Dr. Lal. "Your skin barrier requires moisture and hydration to stay healthy," he adds, noting that all skin types should load up on formulas rich in ceramides, glycerin, and hyaluronic acid. “A moisturizer also helps trap in all the products underneath it to make the ingredients even more effective," adds Dr. Idriss.

You can use the same moisturizer morning and night, FYI. But some might prefer a lighter-weight option in the morning, or one that combines SPF for a lil two-in-one action. Oily skin should look for lightweight moisturizers in a gel-based formula to keep skin hydrated without feeling greasy.

The best dry-skin moisturizers “should be filled with all the things your body naturally produces and can use more of, like hyaluronic acid, lipids, and proteins,” says Dr. Gohara. Cream-based formulas will be your BFF, morning and night.

If you want, you can tiptoe into the retinol game by using an anti-aging night cream in the p.m., which usually has a gentler, “watered-down” dose of retinoids. That being said, it’s often easier—and less irritating—to use your regular moisturizer and layer a retinol on top (see: the next step).

“Retinoids—the general term for all vitamin-A derivatives, including retinol—sink into your skin to speed up cell turnover, causing your body to churn out fresher, smoother, less-wrinkled skin over time,” says Dr. Gohara. Remember that retinoids take four to six months of consistent use to give you results, so using it every day is key.

But just because it might take half a year to see your wrinkles smooth out doesn’t mean you won’t see more immediate results in other ways. “Retinoids trigger collagen production and cellular exfoliation,” adds Dr. Gohara, “which means they’ll also fade dark spots, smooth scars, clear pores, prevent breakouts, and brighten skin.” Basically, retinoids are the best multitasking product dermatologists recommend.

All retinoids aren't created equal. In order of most powerful to least, it starts with prescription-strength retinoids (like tretinoin), adapalene (which is prescription-strength but sold over-the-counter), retinal (or retinaldehyde), and then retinol. There are also a ton of over-the-counter derivatives of vitamin A in addition to retinal and retinol.

The more sensitive or dry your skin, the weaker your retinoid should be. That, or you'll need a longer acclimation period to get used to it (more on that in a sec). You can also find over-the-counter retinoids paired with anti-inflammatory ingredients, such as niacinamide, to offset their side effects.

If you’re new to retinoids, make sure to start slow to mitigate the initial adjustment period of flakes and sensitivity. “Apply a pea-size drop to your entire face one night a week for one week, then two nights a week for two weeks, then three nights a week for three weeks, and then every other night indefinitely,” says Dr. Gohara.

And if you do have extra-sensitive skin, apply a layer of moisturizer 10 minutes before and 10 minutes after your retinol to reduce irritation without totally diluting the treatment. Think of it like sandwiching your face in moisture.

If you’re already using (or planning to use) a night cream with retinoids, doubling up won’t make the anti-aging results more effective—it’ll just cause inflammation. And if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, retinol is also off-limits.

Sunscreen (of at least SPF 30+) is the absolute last step—and perhaps the most important. “Sunscreen is there to protect your face and act as armor against the outside world,” says Dr. Gohara. “Basically, it’s not adding anything to your skin—it’s protecting your skin.”

And before you tell yourself that the SPF 15 in your foundation is good enough, know this: “The absolute bare minimum SPF you need on your face is SPF 30,” says Dr. Gohara. Unless you’re cool with premature aging, worsened acne scars, and an increased cancer risk.

Sunscreens come in a ton of different formulations nowadays. No more of the gloopy, uncomfortable SPFs from childhood! If you have oily or acne-prone skin, for instance, you might prefer sunscreen with chemical filters, since these feel lightweight on skin and sink in quickly. If your skin is dry, look for a formula with hyaluronic acid or ceramides, as these help skin retain moisture as you wear it.

If you're prone to sensitivities, reach for a mineral-based sunscreen. These use either titanium dioxide, zinc oxide, or both to sit on skin and shield UVA and UVB rays—and, since they don't actually penetrate skin, tend to be less likely to cause reactions than their chemical counterparts. Otherwise, go with a formula that you'll be comfortable slathering on every! single! day!

After all, "sunscreen not only reduces your risk of skin cancer, but it also prevents the formation of abnormal collagen and elastin," says Dr. Lal. Basically, a layer of sunscreen today helps prevent 65-year-old you from having thick, mottled, leathery skin.

Again, "the best sunscreen is the one you'll actually use every day," says Dr. Lal. But your skin will look and feel its best with two separate products. "Moisturizers formulated with sunscreen can be more sensitizing and won't have as many moisturizing benefits," he says. So, like, it's better than nothing, but it's not ideal.

The order of your skincare routine, as well as how and when you apply your skincare products, can make a huge difference in your results. Think about it: If you apply a lightweight serum on top of a rich moisturizer, you're likely not going to experience much from that serum, since it can't penetrate into your skin. But this specific order also can help avoid potential skin irritations and breakouts, like when combining ingredients that can't be used together (i.e., retinol and vitamin C).

You can start a skincare routine at any age. In fact, the sooner you start, the better, says dermatologist Dr. Cheung. "You’re never too young to start protecting your skin," she notes. If you're a beginner, start with the above routine (cleanser, moisturizer, SPF—the holy trinity, IMO), and slowly add additional products depending on what your skin needs.

#6759. Designers Say This ’70s-Inspired Design Trend Is Making a Glamorous Comeback

Get ready to see this glossy finish everywhere again.

We all know design is reflective. Whether it’s in our personal style, architectural splendor, or cultural ties, great design mirrors the world around us. Now, it’s time for it to mirror itself.

Once dismissed as a tacky, ’70s-era trend (not unlike wood paneling), mirrored surfaces are making a comeback. But don’t worry—today’s mirror craze moves past the floor-to-ceiling panels of the past, opting instead for accents that add light, depth, and dimension.

“I love mirrored surfaces in interiors because they can be so transformative & work in all styles. They can add glitz and glamour, especially when you add beveled details,” says Bridget Tiek of TIEK BYDAY. “I love to see mirrors as a backbar, behind shelves, on doors, ceilings and on walls. Basically everywhere!”

Bolder than traditional ready-to-hang mirrors, mirrored surfaces are often hard to place tastefully. Here’s how designers have brought the striking detail into interiors.

Queer Eye for the Straight Guy star Carson Kressley’s Murray Hill apartment is full of personality, and his sunken living room has several glittering surfaces. The designer embraces mirrored shine as a bold accent, as seen in this disco-ball-tiled end table.

Designer Alexander D. Wilson brought a mirrored backsplash into this Upper East Side apartment to elevate the elegant yet fun palette while creating the illusion of a larger space. NYC apartments often feel like a shoebox. With this classic design trick, they don’t have to look like it.

Interior designer Sarah Vaile brought Manhattan to the Windy City in this punchy coastal home. After coating the walls in Farrow & Ball’s Borrowed Light for a classic Nancy Meyers-esque aesthetic, she framed a nearly ceiling-high mirror in crisp white molding, transforming the panel into a bold decorative piece that amplifies space and cosmopolitan chic.

Bold enough to make a fierce statement in even the smallest piece, interior designer Amy Courtney brought industrial flair to her New York City home with a silvery domed lamp to complement the bold hues of her living room’s palette.

While the glassy, expansive nature of mirrored panels certainly has its charms, if you’re hoping to bring both glossy and textured flair to your design, mirrored tiles are the perfect solution. Designer Shannon Ggem used mirrored tiles in this moody bar design to bring more light to the room without sacrificing the deep-hued palette.

While most rely on millwork to bring style to the walls, designer Michelle Prentice opted for mirror panels on the closet doors of this South Carolina bedroom. Not only do they add depth to the design, but they bring a boutique feel while adding to the visual palette and playing off the centered vanity mirror to unify the wall treatments.

As stainless steel fades from an industry standard to a passing fad, designers are getting creative when it comes to finding chic alternatives. In this monochrome green butler’s pantry, designer Bridget Tiek brought in a glassy paneled door to elevate the appliance design, taking the invisible kitchen trend to new heights.

#6758. Warren Beatty and Annette Bening’s Former L.A. Mansion Lists for Nearly $15 Million

The Hollywood power couple custom-built the gated Beverly Hills house.

The longtime Beverly Hills home of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening will soon hit the market, ELLE Decor can exclusively reveal. The married couple custom-built the gated residence in 1992 and raised their four kids there. The stars are one of Hollywood’s most famous power couples: Beatty has received 14 Academy Award nominations, winning for Best Director in 1982, and three Golden Globe Awards, while Bening has received five Oscar nominations, including Best Actress for 1999’s American Beauty, for which she won the Golden Globe.

The A-list actors parted with their longtime property in 2012, selling it for $6.7 million, per Zillow. Its new asking price will be $14.995 million.

The nine-bedroom estate’s current owners—hotelier Jonathan Baker and his wife, Jenny—acquired the property directly from Beatty and Bening, then spearheaded a $5 million renovation that concluded in 2019. They modified the Mediterranean-style home to have a more contemporary feel, with minimal moldings, glossy surfaces, modern furnishings, and bold splashes of color.

However, they still paid homage to the estate’s movie-star pedigree, creating what they call the “Warren Beatty Theater,” a 17-seat screening room in what was once Beatty’s home office.

Other nods to the legendary actor—who starred in classics like Bonnie and Clyde, Dick Tracy, and Bulworth—included integrating his drop-down projection screen into the new living room. Additional perks include a wine room with a suspended-wire storage system, a wood-paneled dressing room with plenty of built-ins, and a network of terraces.

The home’s amenities continue on the manicured grounds, which feature an infinity-edge pool, a lighted tennis court, multiple al fresco entertaining areas, and a separate guest house.

The couple are parents to four children, among them Ella Beatty, who is following in her parents’ acting footsteps and recently played Lizzie Borden in the Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.

The Beverly Hills house will be listed for $14.995 million with Cory Weiss of Douglas Elliman and Jacob Greene of the Altman Brothers at Douglas Elliman.

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#6756. Hailey Bieber’s 30 Best Looks in Honor of Her 30th Birthday

From polka dots and fur to red-carpet statements

Happy birthday, Hailey Bieber! The star has officially turned 30, and to mark another turn around the sun, she kicked off a week of celebrations with a new navy-blue Rhode drop, a festive campaign, and an intimate video series that followed a week in her life. Throughout the vlogs, we saw the founder in fittings and makeup chairs, spending time with son Jack Blues, and reflecting on the past decade. “Becoming a mom definitely changed me the most in my twenties,” she told the camera. “I always knew I wanted to be a mom, I always knew I wanted kids, and it just totally transforms you as a person for the better.”

Of course, the birth-week celebrations have also come with a wardrobe to match. From shearling coats to archival statements, she ushered in the new season with everything from an ivory satin Oriori coat trimmed in gray-white fur to a black silk Armani Privé Fall 2005 set to a Yohji Yamamoto Spring 1998 jacket previously seen on Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy. And we did not expect anything less from the star.

Throughout the years, Bieber has become as known for her style as for her Rhode lipgloss phone cases, playing with understated “quiet luxury,” classic Los Angeles athleisure, and tons of Saint Laurent leather. As she grew from a teenage model into a business owner and, later, young mother, her taste has evolved over time—but through it all, she has given us some major fashion inspiration.

So, in honor of her 30th birthday, we rounded up our 30 favorite looks from the star. And between her plethora of Met Gala ensembles, polka-dot prints, and mismatched moments with husband Justin, there was a lot to pick from.

For the New York Times Dealbook Summit, Bieber takes a page from Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy and wears a Yohji Yamamoto Spring 1998 jacket previously worn by the late It girl.

Stepping out in New York City, Bieber pairs her Phoebe Philo cropped fur coat with blue jeans and vintage Manolos.

The star wears the coat of the season: Conner Ives’s reconstituted fur robe in white silk mikado.

Bieber wears an iridescent jacket from Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel Fall 2026 collection. With a medley of silver, red, and turquoise mesh, the piece puts an aluminum chainmail twist on the house’s signature tweed.

For the Academy Museum Gala, Bieber wears a custom bubblegum-pink Chanel dress.

At the 2026 Vanity Fair Oscar after-party, she hits the carpet wearing a shimmering leopard-print gown, made custom by Armani Privé. She accessorizes with Lorraine Schwartz jewelry and Manolo Blahnik heels.

While in Tokyo, Bieber wears a textured Issey Miyake egg-carton skirt suit from the Fall/Winter 2000 collection.

Doing press in Australia, Bieber wears a green Valentino Spring 2026 minidress, with structured shoulders, ruching, and a sweet bow at the hem.

Bieber attends the GQ Men Of The Year party in a naked dress and sparkly Gucci thong, bringing back the ’90s trend.

At the 2025 Academy Museum Gala, Bieber steps out in a striking, sculptural gown from Schiaparelli, constructed from brown moiré vintage ribbons for the house’s Spring/Summer 2025 Haute Couture runway.

Supporting Kylie Jenner at the Kylie Cosmetics anniversary event, Bieber looks to Wiederhoeft for a belted satin midi dress, designed with a chunky belt and thigh-high slit.

While out for an evening in New York, Bieber turns heads in an electric green minidress from Dolce & Gabbana’s 2003 collection.

Stepping out in New York, Bieber embraces two of the year's biggest trends—polka dots and capris—all in one go.

Bieber wears a Marine Serre dress made out of metallic-silver watch straps for a weekend in Miami during the Grand Prix.

Bieber spends an NYC evening at Cafe Zaffri, wearing a silky ice-blue minidress—a vintage Gucci piece from the fashion house’s Spring/Summer 1998 collection, designed by Tom Ford.

Leaving Funk in Los Angeles with Justin, Hailey is seen in an oversized gray suit with strong shoulders and baggy trousers, paired with a burgundy tie and matching clutch.

Stepping out with Justin, who matches his wife's Adidas with a pop of red, Hailey layers on the leopard print patterns—pairing a matching trench and shoulder bag from Saint Laurent.

Bieber highlights her bump with a silky white asymmetrical minidress and matching square-toe heels.

For her pregnancy announcement, Bieber poses in a bridal long-sleeve Saint Laurent maxi dress and matching lacy veil, with chunky sunglasses for a full old Hollywood glam look.

Captured in what have since become iconic photos, Hailey and Justin take couples dressing to new contrasting heights, with her in a little red dress and him in a gray hoodie and Crocs.

#6754. I'm a Mom of Two, and This Ernesta Rug Gives Me That Luxe Look With the Easy Cleanup of a Washable Option

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I have to admit, I have a bit of a gripe with washable rugs. For years, the design industry has been trying to convince us that the answer to a beautiful, livable home is a washable rug. And while I understand the appeal, especially as a mom to two young kids, a dog, and a household that sees its fair share of spills, muddy shoes, and general chaos, I’ve just never been entirely sold on the idea.

While washable rug options have definitely improved over the years, there’s still something about the weight, texture, and character of a traditional rug that I find hard to forgo for the sake of washability. I want a rug that feels substantial underfoot, looks better with age, and doesn’t require me to wrestle an eight-by-ten-foot piece of fabric into my washing machine every time someone spills a juice box.

When I learned about Ernesta’s protective rug treatment, I was intrigued. The custom rug brand offers an optional treatment designed to help repel spills and make everyday messes easier to clean, without requiring you to compromise on your rug’s style, material, or size. In theory, it offers the best of both worlds: the look and feel of a beautifully made rug, with a little extra insurance against the realities of family life. Plus, it’s a treatment that’s typically hard to access on your own without going custom through a designer.

I actually have several Ernesta rugs in my home (I’m a huge fan of their quality and approachable customization options!), but after swapping in an Ernesta rug treated with the brand’s protective finish in our living room, I don’t think I’ll ever go back to ordering a rug without it. Here’s what you should know about the treatment, how it's held up in my own home, and why I think it may be a smarter investment than yet another washable rug.

Best for: This rug is an excellent option for families, pet owners, or anyone who just prefers not to have to be too precious with their things.

Not ideal for: Anyone looking for a quick-ship rug option.

Bottom Line: The customization of Ernesta’s rug assortment makes it easy to get the exact look and function that serves your home best, including different sizes, non-slip bases, and protections.

One of the reasons I love Ernesta so much is how approachable they make the ordering process. There’s no visiting a showroom or making 400 phone calls to try to get the right custom-cut size. You simply log on to their site, browse the options, then choose up to five samples to try for just $10.

My samples came incredibly quickly—within a few days, they were at my doorstep, ready for review. Because I already liked the look of the rug we had in our living room (more on that later), I knew I didn’t want to stray too far from the neutral, functional foundation it gave us.

When we started, we had Ernesta’s Emerson sisal rug in the space. The nubby texture and color looked beautiful, but it was a bit small (it was originally sized to an old home that we have since moved from), and the deeper grooves of the weave made it hard to clean up spills. I have two young kids and a dog, and truly not a day goes by where someone hasn’t spilled yogurt or cracker crumbs or juice on the rug.

Still, I don’t think you should have to sacrifice beauty for function in a family home, and Ernesta helped us find that balance. After debating between a few different styles, I ended up settling on the Cally wool flatweave rug in Camel. Wool flatweave rugs are notoriously durable on their own, and I knew the protective coating would only help it hold up better. Bonus: The tighter weave meant fewer nooks and crannies for gunk to get into.

Once we decided on our new style, we measured out the size we’d need, which ended up being around 13 x 15 feet. I loved how easy it was to order the exact size we needed for our space, especially given that it wasn’t a standard measurement. If you’re unsure about the right size for your rug (or how many legs of your furniture should be on the rug at one time), Ernesta has helpful guidance on their site.

Placing the order was easy; you can opt into the protective treatment before adding the order to your cart, as well as choose other details, like the type of edge binding and whether you’d like to include a rug pad (we chose the attached version).

Protective treatments for rugs are nothing new; they’ve been available to design industry insiders for years. That said, very few DTC companies offer the treatment, unless you’re buying through a designer or want to seek out a supplier on your own.

That’s what’s so great about Ernesta’s offerings—it’s literally as easy as checking a box before you add your rug to cart. The treatment starts at $62 and increases depending on the size of your rug. Their formula is non-toxic and works by acting as a protective layer between the surface of the rug and any spills or debris, preventing stains from setting in and keeping the fibers intact for longer.

Receiving and installing our Ernesta rug couldn’t have been easier, especially considering its large size. It was delivered and placed in our entryway, where it waited for a few days until my husband and I had a spare moment to lay it out.

The rug was packaged beautifully, with thick plastic wrapping protecting the roll, a firm cardboard tube at the center, and fabric wrapping the edges so the binding didn’t get roughed up in transit. I thought this was a particularly nice touch.

As with most rugs, the corners were a bit flared when we first unrolled it, so here’s my favorite tip: add several ice cubes to any corner you want to lay flat and let them melt. The slow dissipation of moisture will relax the rug's fibers, and by the time it has melted away completely, you should have a totally flat rug.

I was immediately impressed by the look and feel of this rug—the wool was so soft and plush, and the rubber mat integrated on the bottom meant it did not budge once we laid it down (though it did make it difficult to reposition when we laid it a little wonky initially, word to the wise). There was no “chemical” smell from the protective treatments, and the fibers still felt just as soft as they did on the sample I received before ordering.

Aesthetically, I love the vibe that this rug brings to the space. It’s soft and plush and cozy, and finally in better proportion with the rest of the room—which is great, because I have a pair of armchairs I won at auction waiting in the wings for their moment. Before, they were floating off the rug and looked odd, but now, they’ll be perfect.

Logically, the protective treatment was 100 percent the right choice for our family. Not even five minutes after laying it out, my three-year-old squished an applesauce pouch on the rug, and it came up with ease. In the month since having it, we’ve definitely put this rug through the paces of family life, and it still looks as good as the day we opened it. Cleaning it is easy, and Ernesta has a whole page on their site dedicated to care instructions, depending on the material your rug is made of.

Overall, this is the ideal solution to me: a rug that looks as good as it performs, and doesn’t require any design sacrifice (or yelling from mom) in the process.

#6752. Cecilie Bahnsen Rethinks the Fleece for Her Second Uniqlo Collaboration

The collection is a Scandi winter balletcore dream.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Cecilie Bahnsen has a cult following for a reason: the Danish designer’s big blooming dresses and dedication to sporty, easy balletcore have been collected in droves by fashion far and wide. So when Uniqlo came calling for her to design a second collaboration, it was time again for the designer to take the reins and merge her playful girlish Scandi style with the utilitarian wearability of the Japanese giant. The collection, which includes womenswear and childrenswear, puts a focus on cozy winter wardrobe dressing and is available now. In it, Bahnsen is rethinking and retooling the classic winter fleece.

For the occasion, Bahnsen spent half a year designing the collection and also collaborated with her friend Fumiko Imano, the artist, to shoot the campaign in Sweden amidst a picturesque landscape. “It was very much about sisterhood, the journey you do of exploring together, and inspiration also from when I’m in the countryside with my son, and we collect flowers, and how we kind of, he sometimes pinned them on his jumper,” Bahnsen tells ELLE of the new collection. “I think it was really kind of that romantic or nostalgic feeling that I wanted to put into the collection. And then there was also this notion of just working with one fabrication and working with the fleece for winter and how you can work this as layering.”

While Bahnsen in particular is known for her flouncy babydoll dresses, when it came to her second collection for Uniqlo, she tells us it was all about “refinement and balance and creating beautiful kind of everyday pieces.” Her personal favorite piece of the lineup is the fleece in the palest shade of soft pastel pink, embroidered with small flowers. “For me, the fleece is such a classic layering piece,” she says. She’s already been wearing it herself for countryside outings. “There’s romance and nostalgia to pink, and I think with this collaboration, it was nice to do the fleece in pink,” she says. “Showing that it could have that femininity to it was special, and it is also that right tone as a super soft pink that I love.”

The entire collection is designed to be layered, and the fleece is at the center of it. There’s a cropped fleece vest, a sheer long T-shirt printed with subtle bouquets of flowers, a floral-embellished fleece skirt and matching socks, gloves, and hats. Bahnsen herself recommends taking a cue from her own runway shows. “I always love a big jumper or a big fleece over a poof-y dress,” she says. “It has both a super boyish vibe to it but also a princess-y, romantic feeling, too, so I love those kinds of contrasts between each other.”

“These are pieces that you want to not just to work for one season, but to be timeless; it’s become about the perfection of these small details that makes it unique and maybe more romantic than what is normally in the Uniqlo collection,” adds Bahnsen. “I feel like the palette has a really Scandinavian winter tone to it, so how do you balance this soft pink into the darker blacks and blues, and kind of build it up, not in a monocomatic way, but really putting the tones and the layering together.” It’s definitely a chicer way to stay warm. The designer’s latest is the ultimate study of form and function.

#6751. Everything We Know About Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s Wedding

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando just said “I do.” On Saturday, November 21, the former Disney Channel star and her drummer fiancé tied the knot in Palm Springs, surrounded by family and friends.

The newlyweds first met on a blind date back in 2021, and have been linked for the five years since. In the time between, they have kept their relationship fairly private and out of the spotlight, simply popping up for the rare red-carpet appearance or supporting one another at a performance. Behind the scenes, the two have proven avid collaborators, working together on Cyrus’s Something Beautiful and Bass Persuades records.

In December of 2025, Cyrus announced her engagement in the subtle (yet not-so-subtle) manner of debuting a chunky gold engagement ring at the Hollywood premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash—letting the shimmering diamond do all the talking.

Despite keeping things out of the public eye, Cyrus offered a rare glimpse into her life with Morando during her Harper’s Bazaar December 2024/January 2025 cover story interview. “He’s very similar to me,” she said of her beau, a drummer for the rock band Liily. “We just don’t take life too seriously.”

Ahead, we take a look at everything we know about Cyrus and Morando’s wedding.

Cyrus and Morando’s wedding ceremony took place in Palm Springs, California. More specifically, it was held at Frank Sinatra’s former home, which was transformed with hundreds of white roses for the occasion. Photos obtained exclusively by DeuxMoi showed the couple exchanging vows by the pool, in front of an intimate crowd of guests.

The couple’s official photos showed the “Can’t Be Tamed” star wearing a white long-sleeve Saint Laurent gown with an open back and long train. She paired the look with an updo, drop earrings, and pointed-toe heels, and had her Jacquie Aiche-designed engagement ring on full display. Standing with her at the altar, Morando wore a classic suit—matching the guests, who were all dressed in black.

At the ceremony—which was officiated by Flaming Lips frontman Wayne Coyne—Cyrus and Morando were surrounded by friends and family. Among the guests were Cyrus’s parents, Tish and Billy Ray, with their respective partners, Dominic Purcell and Elizabeth Hurley.

#6746. Miley Cyrus Turns to Saint Laurent’s Anthony Vaccarello for a Backless Wedding Dress

The star married Maxx Morando in Palm Springs

Miley Cyrus is a bride—a Saint Laurent bride, that is. Yesterday, the “Wrecking Ball” singer married longtime partner Maxx Morando at an intimate, flower-covered Palm Springs ceremony.

In new photos shared directly by Cyrus, the woman of the hour was seen wearing a timeless white gown, designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent. The whole dress was crafted from silk, and featured long sleeves, an open plunging back, and a train that pooled at her feet. Styled by Bradley Kenneth, it was paired with a matching set of silk slingback heels.

The decision to work with Saint Laurent was not unexpected, given Cyrus’s long-standing partnership with the house. Most recently, the star was seen in Vaccarello’s designs at the 2026 Golden Globes and during her Hollywood Bowl shows in October. The wedding dress, however, was likely one of the creative director’s final big moments with the label, as his departure was announced last month.

For glam, Cyrus went bold, styling her hair in an updo and giving her eyes a smokey shadow. Her stack of diamonds was the perfect blend of classic glamour and rockstar edge (the best of both worlds, if you will), with drop Chopard earrings, studs, and a crawler that curved upward along the ear.

Morando, too, wore Saint Laurent. Sitting next to his wife on a leather chair, he was seen in a black single-breasted tuxedo with a silk-satin tie. He added in his own rockstar edge with a pair of grained-leather sneakers and sunglasses.

A first look at the ceremony, obtained exclusively by DeuxMoi, showed the couple—who first started dating back in 2021, after being set up on a blind date—standing amongst white roses. #6743. Azzedine Alaïa Changed Fashion on His Own Terms

A new exhibition showcases 80 garments from the rule-breaking designer.

In the 1980s, Azzedine Alaïa acquired a title that followed him for the rest of his career: the “King of Cling.” The moniker was a fitting one: the Tunisian couturier was renowned for his sculptural, body-centric designs. He experimented with stretch jersey and “anti-stress” fibers to sculpt the body without restricting movement.

But the nickname was also limiting, failing to capture the full scope of his work. The first major U.S. retrospective devoted to Alaïa, “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, brings his broader legacy into focus through 80 garments and selections from his personal collection of historic fashion.

“As my research went on, I came to realize how important the U.S. market was in Alaïa’s launch,” Laura L. Camerlengo, co-curator of the exhibit and curator in charge of Costume and Textile Arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, tells ELLE. “By the [brand’s] third season, the U.S. was the second highest market after France, [with interest from] both luxury department stores and small independent retailers.”

The exhibition took shape after Camerlengo reached out to Olivier Saillard, director of the Fondation Azzedine Alaïa in Paris, who became her co-curator. As visitors enter the Legion of Honor’s Rosekrans Court, they encounter a dress designed for Grace Jones: a spring/summer 1986 haute couture look that Jones modeled on the runway and wore to the 1985 Oscars de la Mode. Part of the opening display, titled “The Women Who Made Alaïa,” it sets the tone for a show that recognizes the muses—both famous and private clients—who wore and supported his work.

Also on view are looks made famous by Rihanna—namely, a sheer red halter gown with a flowing train that she wore to the 2013 Grammys—and Tina Turner, whose silk-organza dress embroidered with gold-tone beads from Alaïa’s spring/summer 1989 concludes the exhibition.

The show then turns to Alaïa’s iconography, as Camerlengo puts it: the bandage dress, his work in denim, and zippered dresses, as well as rare, lesser-seen gems. “I was really keen to have early works on view, particularly the pieces from the 1980s, when he was launching his brand,” the curator says. “These are pieces that would have been shown at Bergdorf Goodman when he had his first fashion show in the United States.”

The exhibition also places Alaïa’s designs in conversation with the museum’s permanent collection. Belle Epoque-style ensembles from his spring/summer 1992 collection appear among 18th-century European paintings and furnishings, including a Canaletto view of Venice and a sofa commissioned for Marie Antoinette.

Alaïa’s own collection of historic fashion, previously shown in the 2023 Paris exhibition “Azzedine Alaïa, couturier collectionneur,” is represented here, too. The gallery includes pieces by fashion houses he admired, such as Lanvin, Chanel, Balenciaga, and Schiaparelli.

Though Alaïa, who died in 2017 at age 82, is remembered for the body-conscious designs that earned him that “King of Cling” title, he was also a renegade in an industry built around constant production. He showed collections only when he felt they were ready—a maverick approach that still resonates today—and had his creations worn by a who’s who of the modeling world, from Naomi Campbell to Gisele Bündchen. Many of his designs were featured in the pages of ELLE over the decades.

“He was someone who pioneered a new way of thinking about fashion,” Camerlengo says. “He was one of the first to question the fashion system and seasonal calendars and the need for trends. He was focused on meticulous craftsmanship and intentionality in design, a sort of precedent to what we think about today, where we are critical of overproduction and overconsumption in fashion.”

“Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion” is on view at the Legion of Honor Museum from Nov. 21, 2026, to Apr. 11, 2027.

Isaiah followed close behind me, tongue unraveling from his mouth. He rubbed himself against my skirt and smeared saliva over it.

Normally, Sam waited by an upturned barrel beneath the pub’s bay windows. He played cards there alone, practiced tricks one of the Colsons had taught him, bothered anyone who passed for a game, tasked to accompany me through the parish at all times. He now toted a small revolver at his hip and had a tendency of spinning it in his fingers whenever a young girl walked by, which was precisely what he was doing at that moment. I heard the revolver clatter on the cobbles and the girls laugh as I slunk out into the foot traffic. The trolley ambled down the street. I’d be aboard it before Sam would notice me.

I lost Isaiah between a horse cart and a woman toting two babies in slings. He barked as I spirited myself away, to the tracks, to the trolley as it passed, my hand on the frame as I moved to step onto it.

As my first foot left the ground, two large hands gripped my waist and pulled me away. I was unceremoniously placed back onto the cobbles. The trolley bell clanged, people alighted and climbed on as it passed, and I was left behind.

“Can’t imagine where you’re headed,” said a chilling, smoky voice. I turned abruptly and found Patrick looking down at me expectantly. “All alone in a no-good town like this.” Before I could respond, he had an arm around me. He escorted me out of the crowd and to a side street, where he could corral me between a brick wall and himself.

I turned, and a growl escaped me. “I’m not a child,” I said between my teeth, stepping closer to him, unintimidated. “I’ll go where I like, whenever it pleases me.”

Patrick rolled his eyes. And Idia be damned, my heart thundered. He wore his cap and coat, just like every other day. Large leather boots laced haphazardly, short brown hair curling at their ends behind his ears, shirt unbuttoned at the throat, revealing a neck spotted in pale freckles, blue eyes impossible to look away from. “Haven’t even been back a full minute, and already she’s testin’ my sanity,” he said to the sky, then placed one hand on the wall by my head and brought his face so close to mine, it was difficult to hold onto my anger. “You agreed to some terms, as I remember it,” he said. My breaths shortened. “You go where you like, so long as you’re guarded.”

“As I remember it, I agreed to those terms under duress,” I hissed back. It was true, in a sense.

“My head between your legs ain’t duress, darlin’.”

I blushed, looked either side of us, but there was too much noise to be overheard.

Patrick grinned. “Nevertheless, you agreed. It ain’t safe to wonder about alone.”

“You’ve been busy most of the time,” I said, meeting his gaze unwillingly. “With all those affairs too dangerous for me.”

He grimaced. “That’s why you have Sam. Or Otto, or Scottie if you prefer.”

At that, the shadows beneath his eyes darkened. “Did they insult you?”

“Patrick,” I said, my tone turning derisive. “Every person here detests me. They don’t need to say it for me to know.”

Patrick straightened. He looked down Main Street, then back at me, deliberating.

I crossed my arms over my chest and waited.

He tilted his head, then held out his hand, and I eyed it like a man had never proffered his hand to me before.

When Patrick did nothing but raise his eyebrows expectantly, I scoffed. “Is that supposed to be my invitation?”

I tightened my crossed arms against my ribcage and lifted my chin.

Patrick smiled down at his boots, then he placed both hands in his pockets and leaned in so his mouth was by my jaw, his breath curling over the shell of my ear, and the gooseflesh of my neck awakened. “Miss Harrow, would you do me the honor of promenadin’ downtown with me?”

His lips barely skimmed over my cheek, and I expelled a breath. “You won’t,” he said assuredly. “You wouldn’t have your gift then.”

He pressed a kiss to the underside of my jaw then stepped away, hiding a smile. “Come on, Scurry girl,” he said. “Give in. Walk with me.”

I shook my head, exasperated, but put my arm in the crook of his and felt suddenly at home. “Not very gentlemanly to bribe a woman.”

“There ain’t a single thing about you that inspires me to be gentlemanly,” he said, pulling me into his side.

We passed Sam, who was leaning against the brickwork of Colson & Sons, a toothpick hanging from his mouth. He pulled a card from behind a young lady’s ear, and her friends giggled and blushed.

“Sammy boy!” Patrick called to him, and the kid had the good sense to flinch, then stand taller. “Cold this mornin’, eh?” Patrick continued. “Not as cold as you’ll be in the boatyard tonight.”

“Best you go home. I hear your mother’s runnin’ you a hot bath for the two of you to share.”

The gaggle of girls went fully red-faced in the presence of Patrick. They scurried away, trapping laughter in their hands.

Sam’s arms rose and fell at his side. “Ah, come on, Patty!” he protested to our receding backs. I was only talkin’ to ’em!”

“Talk to the rats in the boatyard,” Patrick said without turning. “Impress ’em with your cards.”

We advanced down Main Street to the sounds of Sam’s faint cursing. The last remnants of winter blew through the alleys, smelling of charcoal and chimney smoke. Snow drifts had given way to puddles. Kenton Hill was beginning to look like itself again, though the tops of some buildings were still blackened and crumbled. Piles of bricks waited at door fronts, and the lanterns that hung overhead sagged. Some dangled precariously off the eaves. Briggs stood on a giant ladder held by two undersized teenagers; he pulled pliers from his back pocket and restrung them one at a time.

But the men too old to mine still sat at their card tables and shouted to each other. Bedsheets hung between the highest floors of townhouses. The lanes filled and emptied with horses, wagons, and all manner of Crafter. On a hill to the east, the dead had been buried and their graves marked. Kenton Hill churned cautiously on. The war raging across the brink hadn’t penetrated the parish again since the invasion of the Lords’ Army. They were each waiting on the day it would.

Each tunnel into Kenton Hill had been caved in at its closest end. It was the first thing Patrick had asked of me after our return. Every direct line to those surrounding parishes, and the diverging paths beyond them had been sealed. “Not a single comrade between us now,” he had said.

Loyalty had held those tunnels up. Now, there wasn’t a lick of it to be found in the brink.

The Kenton Hill miners came to Colson & Sons in the evening and spoke of hearing shovels on the other side of the walls. Some said it was paranoia. Patrick said it was more likely brigades of angry men, picking at the dirt in some last spasm of futility.

The newsprint continued to flame the ire. The House reported “progress” in their new partnership with the chair of the Miners Union. The members throughout the brink either threw down their weapons or threw up their hands, and as far as the press was concerned, Patrick and I had given the House a seam of terranium so large, it could power generations of Artisans for the foreseeable future, and we’d done so for handsome compensation.

John Colson, the first chairman of the Miners Union—the one each member had followed into the rebellion—was dead.

His son, Patrick, had sold the movement for coin. He was a swank lover. A turncoat.

The Miners Union was done. That was the news of the day.

Every evening, I closed my eyes and pictured Terrence Shop standing overhead, watching us run about our mazes, stumbling into traps, gnawing through the walls.

Patrick saw me shudder and pulled his coat off.

He ignored me. The coat was draped over my shoulders, and he was left in just his trousers, suspenders, his white buttoned shirt, the chill passing through his clothing with little effect. His breath fogged the air. “Gave my coat to a girl when I was fifteen,” he grinned. “Thought it’d win her over for sure.”

“She ran off with it,” Patrick said. “With the coins in the breast pocket.”

I tsked. “And who had you stolen the coins from?”

“Donny,” he said. “Who stole ’em from our dad.”

Patrick shrugged his shoulders. “Weren’t much point. He could always tell when we were lyin’.” His mouth closed in a hard line, his expression closing at the mention of his father.

It wasn’t a topic I’d yet been able to touch. John had betrayed him in the worst ways a father could.

So, Patrick had shot him between the eyes.

There had been no funeral. No remarks other than to explain to his brothers that the man’s name would never be mentioned again.

The subject, I knew, wasn’t to be broached. It was to be accepted: Patrick had killed his father, just as he’d said. There wasn’t anything more to know.

I looked up at him as we strolled, my fingers trailing down his forearm. “You must feel . . . conflicted,” I ventured carefully. “I know you respected him.”

Patrick’s extremities stiffened, something withheld in their channels. His face turned shadowed, his irises crystalized. “Show me a place where conflict ain’t,” was all he said.

I chewed on my tongue for a moment. “What . . . what exactly happened when—”

“Patty!” someone shouted. A man with a thick mustache and a waist apron was weaving his way through pedestrians on the street side. He heaved great breaths as he approached. “There’s fightin’ at the market!”

Patrick’s brow creased and he swore beneath his breath. “Who?”

“That Hal lad and . . .” The man hesitated. “The Charmer boy.”

Patrick closed his eyes. “What are my chances of gettin’ you back to the hotel?”

He muttered something I couldn’t hear. “Keep up then, darlin’.” He wrapped one hand around mine and pulled me along. “No earthquakes today. I mean it.”

#6732. Quick Refresher on Ariana Grande’s Full Dating History Over the Years

Including Dalton, Ethan, Pete, Mac, and Ricky’s surprise round two.

Ariana Grande has been in the spotlight since she was a teenager, meaning her private life has never exactly been all that private. Ariana has been pretty open about sharing her relationships over the years, and they’ve been the source of inspiration for some of her best songs (“thank u, next,” anyone?).

Check out everyone Ariana has dated—from her ex-husband Dalton Gomez, to her whirlwind Wicked showmance with Ethan Slater, to her second-chance romance with Ricky Alvarez.

Graham and Ariana starred in the Broadway musical 13 and apparently started dating while working together. They’re still friends, and Graham came to Ariana’s defense during Doughnut Gate, saying, “She’s such a sweet girl. It’s tough. We all say things that we regret. I don’t think it speaks to her character at all.”

TBD how often Graham and Ariana hang out these days, but they had a 13 reunion back in 2016:

And in 2019, they were spotted going to celeb hot spot Carbone.

Ariana briefly dated Victorious backup dancer Jordan following her split from Graham, with their romance lasting just about a year before they split in February 2012.

At the time, Ari told Just Jared Jr. that her “heart was broken and shattered,” adding, “I was crying through hair and makeup, like I couldn’t even pull myself together.”

After briefly dating in 2012 (side note: Jai accused Ari of cheating with Nathan Sykes, which she denied), these two got back together in 2014 only to break up again.

A source told Us Weekly, “It has not been an easy few months. Jai just wasn’t as supportive as he could have been.”

Ariana dated The Wanted’s Nathan Sykes in 2013—around the time their song “Almost Is Never Enough” (which I definitely still fully listen to on repeat) debuted.

According to People, Ariana confirmed their split in January 2014, saying they ended things because of distance. The ’ship doesn’t appear to have made too much of a lasting impression on Ariana, because Nathan was not name-dropped in “thank u, next,” which he told TMZ was “good.”

Meanwhile, a source told Us Weekly, “They made the decision to part ways because their conflicting touring schedules would keep them apart over the next year.”

And, yes, for all of you wondering, Big Sean was indeed name-checked on “thank u, next,” when Ariana sang, “Thought I’d end up with Sean / But he wasn’t a match.”

Ricky and Ariana dated during her aforementioned Doughnut Debacle and got close when he was working as one of her backup dancers. A source told E! News re: their split, “She broke up with him. He didn’t cheat or anything. They just found it difficult to make it work. They are still friends though.”

According to Victoria Monét, the song “Moonlight” is about a romantic night Ariana and Ricky shared.

“That’s what Ricky called her one night. I think it was after their first kiss,” she told Billboard. “He wanted to kiss her for a long time, and she was really impressed. He’s such a gentleman, and the song is a great little bookmark of the start of their relationship.”

P.S. Here’s Ricky reacting to the “thank u, next” lyrics “Wrote some songs about Ricky / Now I listen and laugh.”

Ariana and Mac Miller dated for two years before parting ways in May 2018.

After Mac’s tragic death in September 2018, Ariana told Vogue in 2019 that “by no means was what we had perfect. He was the best person ever, and he didn’t deserve the demons he had. I was the glue for such a long time, and I found myself becoming...less and less sticky. The pieces just started to float away.” Over the years, she’s penned songs alluding to their relationship, from “Better Off” to “Ghostin.’”

Who can forget the whirlwind relationship that was Pete and Ari? The matching tattoos! The Starbucks cups! The lollipops! This!

It was all a lot! But after a fast-moving few months that included an engagement, Pete and Ariana parted ways in October 2019.

A month later, he told Paper magazine, “I don’t ever make public statements about relationships ’cause I just don’t think it’s right, you know? I usually express how I feel about anything through work. So I hope she’s well. I hope she’s very happy. And that’s pretty much it. And print doesn’t usually age well.”

Ariana and Social House’s Mikey Foster sparked dating rumors thanks to their vibes in this music video:

But it was short-lived, and they ended things in early 2020—before Ariana started seeing Dalton Gomez. Which brings us to...

Ariana and Dalton got together right around the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and by December 2020, they were engaged. The two then tied the knot in May 2021 at her Montecito home, and all seemed to be going well...until just about two years later, when their split was announced.

TMZ broke the news that Ariana and Dalton had been separated since January 2023 and were “heading toward divorce” in July 2023, with sources saying distance (at the time, Ariana had been in England filming Wicked) played a big part. In September 2023, the couple officially filed for divorce.

To the shock of many/all, TMZ reported that Ariana was dating her Wicked costar Ethan Slater shortly after her split from Dalton Gomez went public. According to Us Weekly, Ariana and Ethan got together after Ethan broke things off with his wife Lilly and after Ariana ended things with Dalton.

A source at the time explained, “Ariana and Ethan are dating. However, things are fairly new. Ariana and Dalton split in January, and Ethan is separated from his wife. Ariana and Ethan have only recently begun seeing each other but they have a lot of fun together and are enjoying each other’s company.”

A whirlwind relationship followed, though in October 2025, breakup rumors began swirling. Still, it wasn’t until June 2026 that TMZ broke the news of their split, with a source claiming they parted ways “quietly” a few months ago.

Which brings us back to Ricky! Soon after the Ethan breakup news dropped, Ari started quietly changing the Ricky lyrics in “thank u, next” during her Eternal Sunshine Tour. Several sightings of the two together followed until, eventually, the couple showed up at the Focker-In-Law premiere together, making clear they are very much back on.
